content.stem: X-rays and gamma rays are both:
content.explanation: X-rays and gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation (photons) with no mass and no charge; they differ in origin, not in fundamental nature.
distractors: Photons carry no electric charge, unlike alpha or beta particles.
Radiation used in RT is electromagnetic, not acoustic like ultrasound.
Neutrons are particles used in neutron radiography, a separate method.

content.stem: The fundamental difference between X-rays and gamma rays is that:
options: X-rays originate outside the nucleus; gamma rays originate within the nucleus
X-rays are particles and gamma rays are waves
content.explanation: X-rays are produced when fast electrons strike a target (outside the nucleus); gamma rays are emitted from the nucleus of a decaying radioactive atom.
distractors: Both are electromagnetic photons, not one particle and one wave.
Gamma rays carry significant energy and penetrate matter.
X-rays readily expose radiographic film.

content.stem: In an X-ray tube, X-rays are produced when:
content.explanation: Electrons boiled off the filament are accelerated by high voltage and strike the target, where their energy converts to X-rays (and heat).
distractors: Cooling the cathode does not generate X-rays.
Film development is a darkroom process, not X-ray production.
Grounding does not produce X-rays.

content.stem: The continuous X-ray spectrum from a tube is produced by:
content.explanation: Bremsstrahlung (braking radiation) gives a continuous spectrum as electrons decelerate near target nuclei; characteristic peaks are superimposed on it.
distractors: Nuclear decay produces gamma rays, not the tube's continuous X-ray spectrum.
Characteristic radiation gives discrete peaks, not the continuous spectrum.
Visible light is not the source of the X-ray spectrum.

content.stem: Characteristic X-rays are produced when:
options: An incident electron ejects an inner-shell electron and an outer electron fills the vacancy
content.explanation: Characteristic radiation appears as discrete energy peaks when an inner-shell vacancy is filled by an outer electron, releasing a photon of energy specific to the target element.
distractors: Simple deceleration produces bremsstrahlung, not characteristic peaks.
Nuclear decay produces gamma radiation, not characteristic X-rays.
Film fluorescence is unrelated to characteristic X-ray production.

content.stem: Increasing the kilovoltage (kV) on an X-ray machine primarily increases the radiation's:
content.explanation: kV controls the energy (quality) of the X-rays, raising their penetrating ability; mA and time control quantity.
distractors: Quantity is controlled mainly by mA and time, not kV.
X-rays from a tube have no half-life; that applies to isotopes.
kV raises penetration and affects density, but density is not unlimited and depends on several factors.

content.stem: Milliamperage (mA) on an X-ray machine primarily controls the:
content.explanation: mA sets the tube current and thus the number of X-rays produced (quantity/intensity); kV sets the energy.
distractors: Energy (penetration) is controlled by kV, not mA.
Half-life applies to isotopes, not an X-ray tube.
Focal spot size is a tube design feature, not set by mA.

content.stem: Which is a common industrial gamma-ray source?
content.explanation: Iridium-192 is a widely used industrial gamma source; Co-60 and Se-75 are also common. The other listed nuclides are stable and non-emitting.
distractors: Hydrogen-1 is stable and not a gamma source.
Carbon-12 is stable and not a gamma source.
Lead-208 is stable; lead is used as shielding, not a source.

content.stem: The approximate half-life of Iridium-192 is:
content.explanation: Ir-192 has a half-life of roughly 74 days, so its output falls noticeably over weeks and exposure times must be adjusted as it decays.
distractors: About 5.3 years is the half-life of Cobalt-60, not Iridium-192.
About 30 years is the half-life of Cesium-137.
120 years is not the half-life of a common industrial source; Se-75 is about 120 days, not years.

content.stem: The approximate half-life of Cobalt-60 is:
content.explanation: Co-60 has a half-life of about 5.27 years, giving it a long usable life and high energy suited to thick steel.
distractors: About 74 days is the half-life of Iridium-192.
About 120 days is the half-life of Selenium-75.
About 30 years is the half-life of Cesium-137.

content.stem: The approximate half-life of Selenium-75 is:
content.explanation: Se-75 has a half-life of about 120 days and a lower average energy, making it useful for thinner steel sections with good sensitivity.
distractors: About 74 days is the half-life of Iridium-192.
About 5.3 years is the half-life of Cobalt-60.
About 30 years is the half-life of Cesium-137.

content.stem: Among common industrial isotopes, which has the highest gamma energy and greatest penetration?
content.explanation: Co-60 emits about 1.17 and 1.33 MeV gammas (roughly 1.25 MeV average), the highest of these, suited to thick steel; Se-75 is the lowest energy.
distractors: Selenium-75 is among the lowest-energy of these sources.
Iridium-192 is intermediate in energy, below Cobalt-60.
Thulium-170 is a low-energy source for thin sections, not the highest.

content.stem: Cobalt-60 emits gamma rays of approximately:
content.explanation: Co-60 emits two gammas at about 1.17 and 1.33 MeV (average near 1.25 MeV), giving high penetration for thick steel.
distractors: About 0.66 MeV is the single gamma energy of Cesium-137.
A spread of about 0.08 to 0.6 MeV is closer to the Iridium-192 spectrum.
0.027 MeV is a very low energy, far below Cobalt-60.

content.stem: Iridium-192 emits a spectrum of gamma energies with an average commonly cited around:
content.explanation: Ir-192 emits many gamma lines (roughly 0.2 to 0.6 MeV) with an average often cited near 0.3 to 0.4 MeV, intermediate penetration suited to common steel thicknesses.
distractors: About 1.25 MeV is the average for Cobalt-60, not Iridium-192.
2.5 MeV exceeds the energy of common industrial gamma sources.
0.01 MeV is far too low for Iridium-192.

content.stem: The activity of a radioactive source is measured in:
content.explanation: Activity (rate of decay) is expressed in curies (Ci) or becquerels (Bq); 1 Ci equals 3.7 x 10^10 Bq.
distractors: Roentgen is a unit of exposure in air, not activity.
Rem is a unit of dose equivalent, not activity.
Volts measure electrical potential, not activity.

content.stem: One curie is equal to:
content.explanation: By definition, 1 curie equals 3.7 x 10^10 disintegrations per second, which is 3.7 x 10^10 becquerels.
distractors: 100 Bq is far smaller than a curie.
1000 Bq is far smaller than a curie.
1 Bq is one disintegration per second, vastly smaller than a curie.

content.stem: As a radioactive source decays, its activity:
options: Decreases over time, so exposure times must be increased
content.explanation: Activity falls as the source decays, so exposure (or source-to-film) settings are adjusted over the source's life to maintain density.
distractors: Activity decreases, not increases, as the source decays.
Activity is not constant; it falls with each half-life.
Activity cannot be negative.

content.stem: Higher specific activity (curies per gram) of a source allows:
options: A physically smaller source, improving radiographic definition
content.explanation: High specific activity packs more activity into a smaller physical size, reducing the effective focal-spot size and geometric unsharpness for sharper radiographs.
distractors: High specific activity yields a smaller, not larger, source.
Specific activity does not change the isotope's half-life.
Source size does not by itself change the isotope's penetrating energy.

content.stem: The physical size of a gamma source is important because it acts like the:
content.explanation: The source's physical dimensions behave like an X-ray focal spot; a larger source increases penumbra (geometric unsharpness) and blurs detail.
distractors: Source size is a geometry factor, not film density itself.
Half-value layer is a material/energy property, not source size.
Developer temperature is a processing parameter, unrelated to source size.

content.stem: An advantage of X-ray machines over gamma sources is that:
options: Energy is adjustable and the radiation stops when powered off
content.explanation: X-ray output can be tuned by kV and switched off entirely, improving control and safety where power is available; gamma sources emit continuously.
distractors: X-ray machines require electrical power.
Gamma projectors are generally more portable than X-ray machines.
X-ray equipment still requires shielding and controls during operation.

content.stem: An advantage of gamma sources over X-ray machines is that they:
options: Are portable and need no electrical power
content.explanation: Gamma projectors are compact, need no power, and reach confined field locations, which is why they are common in pipeline and field radiography.
distractors: A gamma source cannot be switched off; it decays continuously.
Gamma sources do not inherently give higher definition; source size and geometry matter.
Gamma sources are a significant radiation hazard requiring strict controls.

content.stem: Because photons have no charge or mass, they:
options: Are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields
content.explanation: Uncharged, massless photons travel in straight lines unaffected by electric or magnetic fields and penetrate matter according to its density and thickness.
distractors: Photons of sufficient energy penetrate metal; that is the basis of RT.
Photons travel at the speed of light, far faster than sound.
Photons carry no charge.

content.stem: Higher photon energy generally results in:
options: Greater penetration through a given material
content.explanation: More energetic photons penetrate further, so higher energy is used for thicker or denser sections.
distractors: Higher energy increases, not decreases, penetration.
Photon energy does not set an isotope's half-life.
Energy and activity are independent properties.

content.stem: A smaller focal spot on an X-ray tube produces:
content.explanation: A smaller focal spot reduces penumbra and geometric unsharpness, improving definition, though it limits how much tube current the target can handle.
distractors: Focal spot size primarily affects sharpness, not scatter level by itself.
Focal spot size does not change the kV.
X-ray tubes have no half-life.

content.stem: Most of the energy delivered to an X-ray tube target becomes:
options: Heat, with only a small fraction becoming X-rays
content.explanation: X-ray production is inefficient; the great majority of the electron energy becomes heat, which is why targets need cooling and duty cycles are limited.
distractors: Only a small percentage becomes X-rays; most becomes heat.
Little visible light is produced relative to heat.
Sound is not a significant product.

content.stem: Cesium-137 emits a gamma of about 0.66 MeV and has a half-life of about:
content.explanation: Cs-137 has a roughly 30-year half-life and a single 0.662 MeV gamma; it is less common industrially than Ir-192 or Co-60.
distractors: About 74 days is the half-life of Iridium-192.
About 120 days is the half-life of Selenium-75.
About 5.3 years is the half-life of Cobalt-60.

content.stem: For radiography of very thick steel, the preferred gamma source is often:
options: Cobalt-60, for its high energy and penetration
Any source, since energy does not matter
content.explanation: Co-60's high energy penetrates thick steel where lower-energy sources cannot produce an adequate radiograph.
distractors: Se-75's lower energy suits thinner sections, not very thick steel.
Thulium-170 is for very thin sections.
Energy strongly affects penetration and must match thickness.

content.stem: For thin steel sections where good sensitivity is needed, a lower-energy source such as Selenium-75 is preferred because:
options: Lower energy gives higher subject contrast on thin material
content.explanation: Lower-energy photons produce more contrast on thin sections, improving flaw sensitivity where high energy would wash out contrast.
distractors: Lower energy penetrates thick steel less, not better.
Se-75 does not have the longest half-life among common sources.
Se-75 is a radioactive emitter; it is not radiation-free.

content.stem: A gamma source is stored and transported in a shielded device commonly called a:
content.explanation: The shielded container that houses the source and lets it be cranked out for exposure is the exposure device, also called a camera or projector.
distractors: A densitometer measures film density, not source housing.
A collimator shapes the beam but is not the storage device.
A cassette holds film and screens, not the source.

content.stem: The flexible cable that connects the source to the drive mechanism in a projector is the:
content.explanation: The source capsule is attached to a pigtail/drive cable so it can be cranked from the shielded position out to the exposure position and back.
distractors: A collimator shapes the beam, not the drive connection.
A densitometer measures film density.
An IQI is an image-quality indicator, unrelated to the drive cable.

content.stem: X-rays and gamma rays are called ionizing radiation because they:
options: Can remove electrons from atoms they interact with
content.explanation: Their energy is high enough to ionize atoms (eject electrons), which underlies both image formation and biological hazard.
distractors: Ionization, not mere heating, defines ionizing radiation.
They do penetrate matter; that is the basis of RT.
X-rays and gamma rays are not visible to the eye.

content.stem: In radiography, radiation 'quality' refers to its:
content.explanation: Quality describes the energy (penetrating power) of the beam; quantity describes the number of photons.
distractors: The number of photons is quantity, not quality.
Film brand is unrelated to radiation quality.
Exposure time affects quantity, not the beam's quality.

content.stem: Photon energy in radiography is commonly expressed in:
content.explanation: Photon energy is given in electron-volts, typically keV or MeV; curies and becquerels measure activity and roentgen measures exposure.
distractors: Curie measures source activity, not photon energy.
Roentgen measures exposure in air, not photon energy.
Becquerel measures activity, not photon energy.

content.stem: If an Iridium-192 source has decayed to half its original activity, a previously correct exposure will need:
options: About twice the exposure time (other factors equal)
content.explanation: With half the activity, roughly double the time is needed to deliver the same exposure, assuming geometry and other factors are unchanged.
distractors: Halving the time would underexpose the film as activity has dropped.
Decay requires adjustment; no change underexposes the film.
kV applies to X-ray machines, not gamma source decay compensation.

content.stem: The source of electrons in an X-ray tube is the:
content.explanation: The filament at the cathode is heated to release electrons (thermionic emission), which are then accelerated toward the target.
distractors: The target (anode) is where electrons strike to produce X-rays, not their source.
A collimator shapes the beam; it does not emit electrons.
Film records the image; it does not emit electrons.

content.stem: An X-ray tube emits a continuous range of energies up to a maximum set by:
content.explanation: The maximum photon energy equals the peak kV; the spectrum is continuous from low energies up to that maximum, with characteristic peaks added.
distractors: mA controls quantity, not the maximum energy.
Film type does not set the X-ray energy.
The developer is a processing chemical, unrelated to the spectrum.

content.stem: Unlike an X-ray machine, a gamma source emits radiation:
options: Continuously and at fixed energies that cannot be adjusted
content.explanation: A gamma source decays continuously at energies fixed by the isotope; you cannot turn it off or tune its energy, only shield it.
distractors: Gamma sources do not require power and cannot be powered off.
Gamma energies are fixed by the isotope, not adjustable.
Gamma sources do emit; they cannot be switched off.

content.stem: The SI unit of radioactivity is the:
content.explanation: The becquerel (Bq), one decay per second, is the SI unit of activity; the curie is the older unit.
distractors: The curie is the traditional (non-SI) unit of activity.
The gray is the SI unit of absorbed dose, not activity.
The sievert is the SI unit of dose equivalent, not activity.

content.stem: Different isotopes are kept available because:
options: Energy must be matched to material type and thickness
Only one thickness is ever radiographed
content.explanation: Source energy is selected to suit the material and thickness for adequate penetration and contrast, so a range of isotopes covers different jobs.
distractors: Sources differ in energy and half-life; they are not identical.
Many thicknesses are radiographed, requiring different energies.
Half-life affects source life and exposure planning, so it matters.

content.stem: Which pairing of source and relative energy is correct?
options: Co-60 high, Ir-192 medium, Se-75 lower
content.explanation: Among these, Co-60 has the highest energy, Ir-192 is intermediate, and Se-75 is lower, which guides thickness selection.
distractors: Se-75 is the lowest, not highest, and Co-60 is the highest.
These sources have distinctly different energies.
Co-60, not Ir-192, has the highest energy of the three.

content.stem: The half-life of an isotope is the time for its:
options: Activity to decay to half its value
content.explanation: Half-life is the period over which activity falls to one half; it is fixed for each isotope and governs source replacement and exposure planning.
distractors: Half-life concerns activity decay, not energy doubling.
Physical source size does not halve with half-life.
Film density is an imaging result, not what half-life measures.

content.stem: After two half-lives, a source's activity is about:
content.explanation: Each half-life halves the activity, so after two half-lives the activity is one half of one half, which is one quarter.
distractors: One half is the activity after a single half-life, not two.
One eighth corresponds to three half-lives, not two.
Activity decreases with each half-life; it does not stay unchanged.

content.stem: Compared with a low-kV X-ray exposure of thin steel, an Iridium-192 exposure of the same part typically gives:
options: Lower contrast because of its higher average energy
content.explanation: Ir-192's higher average energy yields lower subject contrast on thin steel than an optimized low-kV X-ray exposure, which is why X-ray is often preferred for thin, critical work.
distractors: The higher-energy gamma source gives lower, not higher, contrast on thin steel.
The two are not identical; energy spectra differ.
Ir-192 will still produce an image, just with lower contrast.

content.stem: When a radioactive source decays, it:
options: Transforms toward a more stable nuclide while emitting radiation
content.explanation: Radioactive decay converts the unstable nucleus toward a more stable state, emitting gamma (and other) radiation in the process.
distractors: Decay reduces activity over time; it does not gain activity.
A source does not become an X-ray tube.
Decay is gradual over the half-life, not instantaneous.

content.stem: A key safety distinction of gamma sources is that they:
options: Cannot be turned off and must be shielded at all times
content.explanation: Because a gamma source emits continuously, it must remain shielded in its device and controlled at all times; it cannot be switched off like an X-ray machine.
distractors: Gamma sources are not energized; they emit by decay regardless of power.
A stored source still emits and must be shielded; it is not harmless.
Gamma sources produce penetrating radiation, the basis of their hazard and their use.

content.stem: As radiation passes through a material, its intensity is:
content.explanation: The beam is attenuated as photons are absorbed or scattered out of it; thicker or denser material attenuates more, which is what forms the radiographic image.
distractors: Intensity decreases through material; it does not increase.
Intensity changes with thickness and density; it is not unchanged.
Radiation energy is not converted to sound.

content.stem: A half-value layer (HVL) is the thickness of material that:
options: Reduces the radiation intensity to one half
content.explanation: One HVL cuts the beam intensity in half; HVL depends on the material and the radiation energy and is a key shielding and exposure concept.
distractors: An HVL halves, it does not double, intensity.
One HVL halves intensity; it does not stop all radiation.
An HVL by definition reduces intensity.

content.stem: For a given material, higher-energy radiation has an HVL that is:
options: Thicker (more material needed to halve it)
content.explanation: Higher-energy photons penetrate more, so more material is needed to halve them; the HVL increases with energy.
distractors: Higher energy needs more, not less, material to halve it.
HVL is never zero for real materials.
Thickness cannot be negative.

content.stem: Two half-value layers reduce the beam intensity to about:
content.explanation: Each HVL halves the beam, so two HVLs give one half of one half, which is one quarter.
distractors: One half results from a single HVL, not two.
One eighth corresponds to three HVLs.
Two HVLs do not reduce intensity to zero.

content.stem: A tenth-value layer (TVL) reduces beam intensity to:
content.explanation: A TVL cuts intensity to one tenth; it is convenient for shielding calculations since each TVL removes 90 percent of the remaining beam.
distractors: Halving corresponds to an HVL, not a TVL.
One hundredth corresponds to two TVLs.
One quarter corresponds to two HVLs.

content.stem: The photoelectric effect is most significant at:
options: Lower photon energies and in higher-atomic-number materials
Energies above pair production threshold only
content.explanation: Photoelectric absorption dominates at lower energies and rises sharply with atomic number, which is why it contributes strongly to contrast on dense materials at low kV.
distractors: Photoelectric absorption falls off, not rises, at very high energies.
There is no interaction at zero energy.
Pair production is the high-energy process, not photoelectric.

content.stem: Compton scattering is the dominant interaction at:
options: Intermediate energies typical of much industrial radiography
content.explanation: Compton scattering dominates across the intermediate energy range common in industrial RT; it produces scattered radiation that degrades image quality.
distractors: The lowest energies favor the photoelectric effect.
Above about 1.02 MeV pair production begins to contribute, but Compton dominates the mid range.
There is no interaction at zero energy.

content.stem: Pair production can occur only when the photon energy exceeds about:
content.explanation: Pair production requires at least 1.02 MeV (twice the electron rest-mass energy) to create an electron-positron pair, so it matters mainly for high-energy sources like Co-60 and high-MeV machines.
distractors: 0.5 MeV is below the 1.02 MeV threshold for pair production.
0.1 MeV is far below the threshold.
10 keV is far below the threshold.

content.stem: Scattered radiation reaching the film generally:
options: Reduces contrast and degrades image quality
content.explanation: Scatter adds a general fog that lowers contrast and sensitivity, so radiographers work to reduce and control it.
distractors: Scatter lowers, not improves, contrast.
Scatter does affect the radiograph by adding fog.
Scatter degrades, not increases, definition.

content.stem: Backscatter from objects behind the film is commonly controlled by:
options: A lead sheet behind the cassette
content.explanation: A lead sheet behind the film absorbs backscatter; a lead 'B' that appears as a light image on the film warns that backscatter is excessive.
distractors: Raising kV can increase scatter, not control backscatter.
Removing filters does not address backscatter.
Development time does not control backscatter.

content.stem: If a lead letter 'B' placed behind the cassette appears as a lighter image on the radiograph, it indicates:
options: Excessive backscatter, and the radiograph may be unacceptable
content.explanation: A light (lower-density) 'B' image means significant backscatter reached the film, signaling that backscatter protection must be improved.
distractors: A visible light 'B' indicates a problem, not correct exposure.
It does not indicate good contrast; it warns of backscatter.
It is unrelated to IQI placement.

content.stem: The inverse square law states that radiation intensity:
options: Decreases with the square of the distance from the source
content.explanation: Doubling the distance reduces intensity to one quarter; this governs both exposure (SFD) and safe standoff distances.
distractors: Intensity decreases, not increases, with distance.
Intensity strongly depends on distance.
The fall-off is with the square of distance, not linear.

content.stem: If distance from a source is doubled, the intensity becomes:
content.explanation: By the inverse square law, intensity scales as 1 over distance squared, so doubling distance gives one over four, that is one quarter.
distractors: One half would be a linear, not inverse-square, relationship.
Intensity falls with distance; it does not double.
Intensity changes with distance, so it is not unchanged.

content.stem: To reduce dose rate to one ninth, an operator should increase distance from the source by a factor of:
content.explanation: Since intensity falls as 1 over distance squared, tripling the distance gives 1 over 3 squared, which is one ninth.
distractors: Doubling distance gives one quarter, not one ninth.
A factor of nine in distance gives 1 over 81, far less than one ninth.
A factor of 81 is far more than needed for one ninth.

content.stem: A denser material of the same thickness will attenuate radiation:
options: More than a less dense material
content.explanation: Greater density means more atoms in the path, so more absorption and scatter and greater attenuation.
distractors: Denser material attenuates more, not less.
Density changes attenuation; it is not the same.
Denser material certainly attenuates radiation.

content.stem: Radiographic image contrast arises from differences in the part's:
options: Thickness and density along the beam path
content.explanation: Variations in thickness and density change local attenuation, producing the density differences on the film that reveal features and flaws.
distractors: Color does not affect radiographic attenuation.
Internal thickness and density, not just surface finish, drive contrast.
Temperature does not form the radiographic image.

content.stem: Build-up refers to:
options: Additional scattered radiation adding to the primary beam in thick sections
content.explanation: Build-up is the extra scattered radiation generated within a thick absorber that adds to the transmitted primary beam, affecting attenuation calculations.
distractors: Build-up is a scatter phenomenon, not a film artifact.
Source decay is a separate activity-loss concept.
Filament aging concerns the X-ray tube, not build-up.

content.stem: A metal filter placed at the X-ray tube port is used to:
options: Absorb lower-energy photons and harden the beam
content.explanation: A filter removes softer (low-energy) photons, hardening the beam and reducing scatter and broad exposure latitude effects, at the cost of some intensity.
distractors: A filter reduces, not increases, scatter.
A filter does not change the set kV.
Filtering is a beam-shaping function, not film development.

content.stem: Collimating the beam helps image quality by:
options: Restricting the beam to the area of interest and reducing scatter
content.explanation: A collimator confines the beam to the region being radiographed, lowering scatter from surrounding material and reducing unnecessary exposure.
distractors: Collimation restricts, not enlarges, the field.
Collimation does not change source activity.
Collimation does not remove the required IQI.

content.stem: Lead masking around a part during exposure is used to:
options: Reduce scatter from radiation passing around the part
content.explanation: Masking absorbs radiation that would otherwise pass around the part and scatter back to the film, improving contrast on the edges and thin sections.
distractors: Masking reduces, not increases, fog.
Masking does not change the kV.
Masking is unrelated to development speed.

content.stem: Major sources of scattered radiation in radiography include:
options: The part, the floor, walls, and nearby objects
content.explanation: Scatter comes from the object and surrounding surfaces; controlling it involves collimation, masking, filters, and backscatter protection.
distractors: The film is not the primary scatter source.
The IQI is a small image-quality device, not a major scatter source.
The densitometer is a measuring instrument, not a scatter source.

content.stem: Lower radiation energy generally produces:
content.explanation: Lower energy increases the difference in attenuation between thicknesses, raising subject contrast, but it penetrates less, so energy is balanced against thickness.
distractors: Lower energy raises, not lowers, subject contrast.
Lower energy still forms an image on suitable thickness.
Lower energy gives less, not more, penetration.

content.stem: Knowing a material's HVL for a given source lets you:
options: Calculate the shielding thickness needed to reach a target dose rate
content.explanation: Successive HVLs each halve the dose rate, so HVL data is used to compute shielding thickness for a desired reduction.
distractors: Film density is set by exposure and processing, not HVL.
Half-life is an isotope property, not derived from HVL.
Developer choice is unrelated to HVL.

content.stem: Lead is widely used for radiation shielding because it:
options: Has high density and high atomic number, strongly attenuating photons
content.explanation: Lead's high density and atomic number make it an efficient absorber of X-rays and gamma rays per unit thickness.
distractors: Lead strongly absorbs, rather than transmits, radiation.
Lead is a shield, not a radiation emitter.
Lead is dense and heavy, which is part of why it shields well.

content.stem: Concrete is often used for facility shielding because it:
options: Provides attenuation in bulk at lower cost for walls
content.explanation: Concrete attenuates radiation and is economical for large structural barriers, though more thickness is needed than for lead.
distractors: Concrete does attenuate radiation.
Concrete is dense, not lighter than air.
Concrete is a shield, not an emitter.

content.stem: Which combination best reduces scatter reaching the film?
options: Collimation, filtration, masking, and backscatter lead
content.explanation: Collimation, beam filtration, masking, and a backscatter lead sheet together limit scatter and improve contrast.
distractors: Raising kV and removing filters tends to increase scatter.
A larger field admits more scatter.
Lead screens help control scatter and intensify the image; removing them is counterproductive.

content.stem: Attenuation of a narrow monoenergetic beam through matter is:
content.explanation: Each layer removes a fixed fraction, so intensity falls exponentially with thickness, which is why HVL and TVL are constant-ratio concepts.
distractors: The relationship is exponential, not linear.
Attenuation strongly depends on thickness.
Attenuation is not zero for real materials.

content.stem: Increasing the source-to-film distance (SFD) will, by the inverse square law:
options: Decrease the intensity at the film
content.explanation: Greater SFD lowers the intensity reaching the film (as 1 over distance squared), requiring longer exposure but improving geometry.
distractors: Greater distance lowers, not raises, intensity.
Distance does affect intensity.
SFD does not change the source's energy.

content.stem: If the chosen energy is too low for the part thickness, the radiograph will likely be:
content.explanation: Insufficient energy fails to penetrate the section, leaving the film underexposed and lacking a usable image of the interior.
distractors: Too little penetration underexposes rather than overexposes.
Mismatched energy does not give a perfect exposure.
Low energy does not eliminate scatter.

content.stem: Using energy higher than necessary for a thickness tends to:
options: Lower contrast and reduce flaw sensitivity
Eliminate the need for an IQI
content.explanation: Excess energy reduces the attenuation differences that create contrast, lowering sensitivity, so energy is matched to thickness.
distractors: Excess energy lowers, not raises, contrast.
An IQI is always required to verify quality.
Excess energy does not improve definition.

content.stem: Side scatter is best reduced by:
options: Collimation and masking around the part
content.explanation: Confining the beam and masking around the part cut side scatter from surrounding material and equipment.
distractors: Removing the cassette would prevent imaging, not reduce scatter.
Raising mA increases quantity, not scatter control.
Fixing time is a processing step, unrelated to side scatter.

content.stem: At low energies, attenuation rises steeply with the material's:
content.explanation: Photoelectric absorption depends strongly on atomic number at low energies, so high-Z materials attenuate low-energy photons much more.
distractors: Color does not affect attenuation.
Surface roughness does not drive bulk attenuation.
Temperature is not the dominant attenuation factor.

content.stem: Compton scattering depends mainly on:
options: Electron density, with little dependence on atomic number
content.explanation: Compton interaction scales with electron density (and so with material density) and is nearly independent of atomic number, dominating mid energies.
distractors: The strong atomic-number dependence belongs to the photoelectric effect, not Compton.
Color is irrelevant to Compton scattering.
Film type does not govern Compton interaction in the part.

content.stem: Controlling scatter is important because uncontrolled scatter:
options: Lowers contrast and can hide discontinuities
content.explanation: Scatter fog reduces contrast and sensitivity, potentially masking real flaws, so its control is central to radiographic quality.
distractors: Scatter degrades, not improves, sensitivity.
Scatter does affect detectability.
Scatter blurs rather than sharpens edges.

content.stem: For personnel safety, the inverse square law means that:
options: Increasing distance rapidly lowers dose rate
content.explanation: Because dose rate falls with the square of distance, stepping back is one of the most effective ways to reduce exposure.
distractors: Distance strongly affects dose rate.
Being closer increases, not decreases, dose.
Dose rate falls, not rises, with distance.

content.stem: Adding one HVL of absorber between source and film requires the exposure to be increased by about:
options: A factor of two (other factors equal)
content.explanation: One HVL halves the transmitted intensity, so roughly double the exposure restores the same film density, all else equal.
distractors: Halving the exposure would underexpose since intensity already dropped by half.
An added HVL reduces transmission, so exposure must change.
A factor of ten corresponds to a tenth-value layer, not a half-value layer.

content.stem: Scatter tends to be a greater problem when radiographing:
content.explanation: Thicker, denser parts generate more scattered radiation, so scatter control is especially important for heavy sections.
distractors: Thin foils generate comparatively little scatter.
An empty cassette is not a radiography subject.
Air produces negligible scatter.

content.stem: The primary (direct) radiation forms the useful image, while scattered radiation:
options: Adds unwanted fog that must be minimized
content.explanation: Only the primary beam carries faithful image information; scatter adds fog, so techniques aim to maximize primary and minimize scatter.
distractors: The IQI image is formed by the primary beam, not scatter.
Scatter does not improve penetration.
Half-life is an isotope property, unrelated to scatter.

content.stem: Which lists interactions roughly from low to high photon energy?
options: All occur only at one energy
content.explanation: Photoelectric absorption dominates at low energy, Compton scattering at intermediate energy, and pair production at high energy (above 1.02 MeV).
distractors: This reverses the energy order of the interactions.
Photoelectric comes before Compton in energy, not after.
These interactions dominate at different energies, not one.

content.stem: Which statement about attenuation is correct?
options: Attenuation increases with thickness and density and decreases with higher energy
content.explanation: More thickness and density attenuate more, while higher energy penetrates more (less attenuation per unit thickness).
distractors: Attenuation depends strongly on energy.
Denser material attenuates more, not less.
Thicker material attenuates more, not less.

content.stem: The main components of an X-ray machine include the:
options: Tube head (with cathode and anode), high-voltage supply, and control unit
content.explanation: An X-ray system has a tube (cathode/anode) in a head, a high-voltage generator, and a control unit setting kV, mA, and time.
distractors: A projector and pigtail belong to a gamma exposure device, not an X-ray machine.
Film and developer are imaging/processing items, not the machine itself.
Survey meters and dosimeters are safety instruments, not the X-ray machine.

content.stem: A constant-potential X-ray unit is characterized by:
options: A nearly steady voltage across the tube for consistent output
content.explanation: Constant-potential units maintain a near-steady tube voltage, giving stable, efficient output useful for consistent industrial exposures.
distractors: Pulsed output describes a different machine type.
X-ray production requires high voltage.
X-ray machines produce X-rays, not gamma rays.

content.stem: A gamma-ray exposure device (projector) functions to:
options: Shield the source and allow it to be driven to the exposure position
content.explanation: The projector stores the source shielded and lets the operator crank it out through a guide tube to the exposure position and back.
distractors: A gamma projector houses a decaying source; it does not generate X-rays electrically.
Film development is a darkroom function.
Dose measurement is done by survey meters and dosimeters.

content.stem: A collimator on a radiographic source is used to:
options: Confine and shape the radiation beam
content.explanation: Collimators restrict the beam to the area of interest, reducing scatter and lowering unnecessary radiation in other directions.
distractors: Collimation does not change source activity.
Collimators do not develop film.
Density measurement is done with a densitometer.

content.stem: Radiographic film consists of an emulsion of:
options: Silver halide crystals on a base, usually coated both sides
content.explanation: Industrial film has light- and radiation-sensitive silver halide emulsion (typically double-coated) on a transparent base; exposure forms a latent image developed into metallic silver.
distractors: Lead foil is a screen material, not the film emulsion.
Phosphor coatings belong to fluorescent screens or imaging plates, not standard film emulsion.
Radiographic film uses a transparent base, not plain paper.

content.stem: Lead foil intensifying screens in direct contact with film:
options: Intensify the image with photoelectrons and absorb some scatter
content.explanation: Lead screens emit photoelectrons that add to the film exposure (intensification) and absorb longer-wavelength scatter, improving quality, when in tight contact with the film.
distractors: Screens assist the film; they do not replace it.
Properly used lead screens improve, not merely fog, the image.
Lead screens improve, not lower, quality when used correctly.

content.stem: Fluorescent (salt) screens differ from lead screens in that they:
options: Emit visible light to expose the film, giving speed but lower definition
content.explanation: Fluorescent screens glow under radiation, greatly increasing speed (shorter exposure) but reducing definition compared with lead screens, so they are used where speed matters more than fine detail.
distractors: Fluorescent screens emit light; that is their function.
Fluorescent screens use phosphor salts, not lead.
Fluorescent screens reduce, not improve, definition versus lead screens.

content.stem: A radiographic cassette holds the:
options: Film and screens in light-tight, close contact
content.explanation: The cassette keeps film and intensifying screens in tight, light-tight contact during exposure to ensure sharp images and proper screen action.
distractors: The source and pigtail belong to the gamma projector.
Developer is held in processing tanks, not the cassette.
The high-voltage supply is part of the X-ray machine.

content.stem: Poor contact between film and intensifying screens results in:
options: Blurred or unsharp areas on the radiograph
content.explanation: Gaps between film and screen let the screen's effect spread, blurring those areas; firm contact is required for sharpness.
distractors: Poor contact blurs rather than sharpens.
Poor contact degrades quality; it does not raise contrast usefully.
Poor contact does affect the image.

content.stem: A densitometer is used to:
options: Measure the optical density of a processed radiograph
content.explanation: A densitometer reads the optical density (degree of film darkening) to verify the radiograph meets density requirements.
distractors: Dose is measured by survey meters and dosimeters, not a densitometer.
The source is driven out by the projector crank, not a densitometer.
kV is set on the X-ray control, not a densitometer.

content.stem: A step wedge or density strip is used to:
options: Calibrate or verify densitometer and viewing performance
content.explanation: A calibrated step tablet provides known densities to verify densitometer calibration and film-viewing conditions.
distractors: A step wedge does not generate radiation.
It does not house a source.
It is a calibration aid, not personnel shielding.

content.stem: A radiographic film viewer (illuminator) must provide:
options: Sufficient, adjustable light to view the required density range
content.explanation: A high-intensity, adjustable illuminator is needed so dense radiographs can be viewed with adequate brightness across the density range.
distractors: Film viewing uses visible light, not ultraviolet alone.
A viewer provides light, not radiation.
No magnetic field is involved in film viewing.

content.stem: In computed radiography (CR), the image is captured on a:
options: Reusable photostimulable phosphor imaging plate, then laser-scanned
content.explanation: CR uses a storage-phosphor imaging plate that holds a latent image; a laser scanner reads it out to a digital image, and the plate is erased and reused.
distractors: Silver halide film is conventional film radiography, not CR.
A lead screen is an intensifying screen, not the CR capture medium.
A fluorescent salt screen is used with film, not as the CR plate.

content.stem: Digital radiography (DR) using a flat-panel detector:
options: Converts radiation to a digital image directly, without a separate scan step
content.explanation: DR flat-panel detectors capture the image electronically and display it on a computer in near real time, without the CR scanning step or film processing.
distractors: DR is filmless and needs no wet processing.
DR relies on an electronic detector.
DR produces a digital image, not film.

content.stem: A general advantage of digital detectors (CR/DR) over film is:
options: No wet chemical processing and easier image storage/transmission
content.explanation: Digital systems eliminate darkroom chemistry and make images easy to store, enhance, and transmit, though equipment cost and technique still matter.
distractors: Digital equipment is not always cheaper; initial cost can be high.
Digital methods still require radiation to form the image.
Digital images can still show artifacts.

content.stem: A source changer is equipment used to:
options: Safely transfer a gamma source to or from a projector
content.explanation: A shielded source changer allows a new source to be loaded into a projector and an old one removed under controlled, shielded conditions.
distractors: Film development is a darkroom function.
Density measurement uses a densitometer.
Exposure time is set on the control or timer, not a source changer.

content.stem: In gamma radiography, the guide tube directs the source from the projector to the:
content.explanation: The flexible guide tube routes the source from the shielded projector out to the exposure head at the part, then the source is retracted afterward.
distractors: The guide tube does not lead to the darkroom.
It does not connect to a survey meter.
It does not connect to a densitometer.

content.stem: The remote crank/drive assembly on a gamma projector exists to:
options: Move the source out and back from a safe distance
content.explanation: The drive cable and crank let the operator position and retract the source from a distance, reducing exposure compared with handling the source directly.
distractors: The crank does not change source energy.
It is not a film-processing device.
Dose is measured by separate instruments.

content.stem: Faster radiographic film generally has:
options: Larger grain and lower definition than slower film
content.explanation: Faster films use larger silver halide grains, shortening exposure but reducing definition; slower, fine-grain films give higher definition at the cost of exposure time.
distractors: Finer grain and higher definition describe slower film, not faster.
All silver halide film has grain.
Grain size and definition are related.

content.stem: Industrial film system classes (per standards such as ASTM E1815) are based primarily on:
content.explanation: Film systems are classified by performance characteristics such as granularity and gradient (contrast and speed), guiding selection for required quality.
distractors: Cassette color does not define the film class.
Source type is independent of film classification.
Developer brand does not set the film class, though processing must match the system.

content.stem: Front and back lead screen thicknesses are selected based on:
options: Radiation energy, to intensify and filter scatter appropriately
content.explanation: Higher energies use thicker lead screens; the front screen filters scatter and the back screen absorbs backscatter, with thickness matched to energy.
distractors: Film color does not determine screen thickness.
Room temperature is unrelated to screen selection.
Half-life does not set screen thickness.

content.stem: Fluorometallic screens combine:
options: A lead foil with a fluorescent layer to balance speed and definition
content.explanation: Fluorometallic screens pair lead and phosphor to gain some speed while retaining more definition than pure fluorescent screens.
distractors: Fluorometallic screens include lead, not only fluorescent salts.
They contain both lead and phosphor.
They are screens, not film or developer.

content.stem: A panoramic (rod-anode) X-ray tube is used to:
options: Expose a full circumferential weld from inside the pipe in one shot
content.explanation: A panoramic tube placed at the center of a pipe exposes the entire circumferential weld at once with the film wrapped outside, improving efficiency.
distractors: It is an exposure tube, not a film processor.
It does not measure density.
It is a source, not shielding.

content.stem: X-ray tubes require cooling because:
options: Most input energy becomes heat at the target
content.explanation: Since the great majority of energy becomes heat, tubes are cooled (oil, air, or water) and operated within duty-cycle limits to avoid target damage.
distractors: Tubes generate substantial heat at the target.
Cooling does not change kV.
Excess heat damages the tube, it does not improve film.

content.stem: Densitometers are periodically verified against a:
options: Calibrated step tablet of known densities
content.explanation: A calibrated density strip with known step values is used to confirm the densitometer reads accurately.
distractors: A survey meter measures radiation, not film density.
A projector houses a source; it does not calibrate a densitometer.
A guide tube routes the source; it is not a calibration standard.

content.stem: Unexposed radiographic film must be stored:
options: Away from radiation, heat, humidity, and chemical fumes
content.explanation: Film is protected from stray radiation, heat, humidity, and fumes, all of which can fog or degrade it before use.
distractors: Storing film near the source would fog it.
Sunlight would expose and ruin the film.
Film is processed in, not stored in, developer.

content.stem: Lead screen intensification is most effective at:
content.explanation: The photoelectron intensification from lead screens becomes effective at higher energies; at very low energies lead screens contribute little intensification.
distractors: At very low energies, lead screen intensification is minimal.
There is no interaction at zero energy.
Lead screens respond to X and gamma radiation, not visible light.

content.stem: A CR imaging plate, after readout, is:
options: Erased by bright light and reused
content.explanation: CR plates are erased with a strong light source after scanning and can be reused many times, unlike single-use film.
distractors: CR plates are reusable, not single-use.
CR uses laser scanning and erasure, not wet chemical development.
CR plates are reusable.

content.stem: Spatial resolution of a DR flat panel is influenced primarily by:
options: Detector pixel pitch and the imaging geometry
content.explanation: In DR, the detector's pixel size and the source/object/detector geometry govern spatial resolution, replacing film grain as the limiting factor.
distractors: Developer temperature applies to film processing, not DR.
DR has no film grain.
Fixing time is a film-processing parameter, not relevant to DR.

content.stem: Selecting between an X-ray machine and a gamma source depends on:
options: Access, power availability, thickness, and quality required
content.explanation: The choice weighs site access and portability, available power, material thickness and energy needed, and the image quality required.
distractors: Selection is technical, not mere preference.
Film color is irrelevant.
Room paint is irrelevant.

content.stem: A microfocus or minifocus X-ray tube is valued for:
options: Very small focal spot enabling high definition and projection magnification
content.explanation: A very small focal spot reduces geometric unsharpness and permits projection magnification techniques, at the cost of limited tube current.
distractors: Microfocus tubes run at low current, not high output.
They emit X-rays, not gamma rays.
They still require shielding.

content.stem: The timer on a radiographic setup controls the:
content.explanation: The timer sets how long the exposure runs, combining with intensity to determine total exposure delivered to the film.
distractors: Source energy is set by kV (or fixed by the isotope), not the timer.
Film grain is a film property, not timer-controlled.
Developer strength is a processing parameter.

content.stem: Lead identification letters and numbers placed on the part appear on the film to:
options: Identify the part, weld, and location for traceability
content.explanation: Lead markers record part and location identification directly on the radiograph, providing traceable identification of what was imaged.
distractors: Identification markers are not personnel shielding.
They do not develop the image.
They do not measure dose.

content.stem: Flexible cassettes are useful for radiography of:
options: Curved surfaces such as pipe welds
content.explanation: Flexible cassettes wrap around curved parts like pipe, keeping film and screens in contact with the contour.
distractors: Rigid cassettes suit flat plate; flexible ones suit curves.
Cassettes hold film, not liquids.
Cassettes do not enclose the source.

content.stem: Added filtration at the tube port is part of the:
options: X-ray equipment configuration to shape beam quality
content.explanation: Filters are mounted at the tube port to harden the beam and reduce scatter, a configurable part of the X-ray equipment.
distractors: Filtration is not a film-processing step.
It is not part of dosimetry.
It is not a darkroom function.

content.stem: Digital radiographic images are archived as:
options: Electronic image files with associated data
content.explanation: Digital images are stored as electronic files (often with technique and traceability data), simplifying retrieval and transmission.
distractors: Digital workflows do not require wet film for archiving.
Images are not stored on lead plates.
They are images, not audio.

content.stem: Intensifying screens must be kept clean because dirt or scratches:
options: Appear as artifacts on every radiograph made with them
content.explanation: Because screens contact the film, any debris or damage reproduces as artifacts on the radiographs, so screens are inspected and cleaned.
distractors: Dirty screens degrade, not improve, contrast.
Screen condition does not change penetration.
Screens are not personnel shielding.

content.stem: A tube rating chart specifies the safe combinations of:
options: kV, mA, and time the tube can handle without overheating
content.explanation: Tube rating charts define allowable kV/mA/time combinations to keep the target within thermal limits.
distractors: Tube ratings concern the tube, not film and developer.
Half-life applies to isotopes, not tube ratings.
IQI sizes are an image-quality matter, not tube ratings.

content.stem: Safety interlocks and warning lights on X-ray enclosures serve to:
options: Prevent exposure when access doors are open and warn when radiation is on
content.explanation: Interlocks shut off the beam if a door opens, and warning lights signal when radiation is being produced, protecting personnel.
distractors: Interlocks do not process film.
They are safety devices, not output controls.
They do not measure density.

content.stem: Which pairing is correct?
options: Densitometer measures film density; survey meter measures radiation; projector houses a gamma source
content.explanation: A densitometer reads film density, a survey meter measures radiation levels, and a gamma projector shields and deploys the source.
distractors: The densitometer does not house a source.
A survey meter measures radiation; it does not develop film.
A projector deploys a source; it does not measure density.

content.stem: The principal X-ray exposure factors are:
options: Kilovoltage, milliamperage, time, and source-to-film distance
content.explanation: Exposure is governed by kV (energy), mA and time (quantity), and the source-to-film distance, which together set film density and quality.
distractors: Developer brand and film color are not the primary exposure factors.
Half-life and activity apply to gamma sources, not X-ray exposure factors generally.
Room conditions are processing/storage concerns, not exposure factors.

content.stem: Radiographic (optical) density refers to:
content.explanation: Optical density is the measured darkening of the processed film; acceptance requires density within a specified range over the area of interest.
distractors: Material density (mass per volume) is a different quantity.
Source activity is measured in curies, not density.
Beam energy is the radiation quality, not film density.

content.stem: For an X-ray exposure, doubling the milliamperage while halving the time will:
options: Keep the total exposure (mA-time) about the same
content.explanation: Total exposure is proportional to mA multiplied by time, so doubling one and halving the other leaves the product, and the density, about unchanged.
distractors: The product is unchanged, not doubled.
The product is unchanged, not halved.
mA and time do not change the kV.

content.stem: Increasing kV (other factors fixed) generally:
options: Increases film density and lowers contrast
content.explanation: Higher kV penetrates more, raising density and exposure latitude while reducing subject contrast, so kV is chosen to balance penetration and contrast.
distractors: Higher kV raises, not lowers, density at fixed mA and time.
kV strongly affects density.
Higher kV lowers, not raises, contrast.

content.stem: If the source-to-film distance is increased, film density (other factors fixed) will:
options: Decrease, following the inverse square law
content.explanation: Greater SFD lowers the intensity at the film as 1 over distance squared, reducing density unless exposure is increased to compensate.
distractors: Greater distance reduces, not increases, density.
Distance changes intensity and thus density.
Density cannot be negative.

content.stem: If SFD is doubled, the exposure must be increased by a factor of about:
content.explanation: Because intensity falls as 1 over distance squared, doubling distance cuts intensity to one quarter, so exposure must be multiplied by four to keep density.
distractors: Doubling exposure only compensates for a factor of about 1.4 in distance, not a doubling.
Halving exposure would worsen the underexposure.
A factor of eight overcompensates for a doubled distance.

content.stem: Subject contrast is determined mainly by:
options: Part thickness/density differences and the radiation energy
content.explanation: Subject contrast comes from how much the part's thickness and density vary along the beam, combined with the radiation energy (lower energy gives more subject contrast).
distractors: Film type affects film contrast, a separate component.
Developer brand is a processing variable, not subject contrast.
Cassette color is irrelevant.

content.stem: Film contrast is a property of the:
content.explanation: Film contrast depends on the film's characteristic curve and how it is processed; radiographic contrast combines subject contrast and film contrast.
distractors: Half-life is an isotope property, unrelated to film contrast.
The collimator shapes the beam, not film contrast.
A survey meter measures radiation, not contrast.

content.stem: Radiographic contrast is the combination of:
content.explanation: Overall radiographic contrast results from subject contrast (part and energy) and film contrast (film and processing) acting together.
distractors: It is not a combination of survey-meter readings.
Source size and half-life are not the contrast components.
Developer temperatures affect processing, not the definition of radiographic contrast.

content.stem: Radiographic definition (sharpness) describes:
options: How sharply detail and edges are reproduced
content.explanation: Definition is the abruptness of the boundaries in the image; it is degraded by geometric unsharpness, poor film/screen contact, and graininess.
distractors: Overall darkness is density, not definition.
Exposure time relates to density, not directly to sharpness.
Source activity is unrelated to definition.

content.stem: Geometric unsharpness (Ug) is calculated as:
options: Ug = F t / d (source size times object-to-film distance over source-to-object distance)
content.explanation: Geometric unsharpness equals the source (focal-spot) size F times the object-to-film distance t, divided by the source-to-object distance d.
distractors: This inverts the relationship.
Unsharpness is a product/ratio, not a sum of the terms.
kV and mA are exposure factors, not the unsharpness formula.

content.stem: Geometric unsharpness is reduced by:
options: A smaller source, greater source-to-object distance, and the part close to the film
Moving the part away from the film
content.explanation: Smaller F, larger d, and smaller t all reduce Ug, so a small source far from the part with the part near the film gives the sharpest image.
distractors: A larger source increases unsharpness.
Greater object-to-film distance (t) increases unsharpness.
Moving the part away from the film increases t and thus unsharpness.

content.stem: For the same geometry, a larger focal spot or source size produces:
content.explanation: Since Ug is proportional to source size F, a larger source increases the penumbra and blurs detail.
distractors: Larger source increases, not decreases, unsharpness.
Source size affects sharpness, not contrast directly.
Source size does change sharpness.

content.stem: Placing the part as close as possible to the film:
content.explanation: Reducing object-to-film distance t lowers Ug, so the part is kept against the film when possible.
distractors: Closeness minimizes, not maximizes, unsharpness.
It does not change the source size.
Object-to-film distance does affect sharpness.

content.stem: Increasing the source-to-object distance, with other geometry fixed:
options: Reduces geometric unsharpness but lowers intensity
content.explanation: A larger source-to-object distance d reduces Ug, but it also lowers intensity at the film (inverse square), so exposure is increased to compensate.
distractors: Greater source-to-object distance reduces, not increases, unsharpness.
Greater distance lowers, not raises, intensity.
Distance does not affect half-life.

content.stem: A radiographic exposure chart relates:
options: Material thickness, kV, and exposure for a given film density and SFD
content.explanation: Exposure charts let the radiographer pick kV and exposure for a thickness to achieve the target density at a stated SFD and film/screen setup.
distractors: Charts relate thickness/kV/exposure, not half-life to film color.
Charts cover exposure factors, not just dose versus distance.
Charts are not developer-to-fixer ratios.

content.stem: Gamma-ray exposures are often expressed in:
content.explanation: Gamma exposure scales with source activity and time, commonly given as curie-minutes; X-ray exposures use milliampere-minutes.
distractors: Milliampere-minutes apply to X-ray machines, not gamma sources.
Kilovolts describe X-ray energy, not gamma exposure quantity.
Becquerel-meters is not a standard exposure unit.

content.stem: The output of a gamma source is sometimes described by its RHM, which is the:
options: Roentgens per hour at one meter for a given activity
content.explanation: RHM (roentgens per hour at one meter) expresses a source's exposure-rate output per unit activity, useful for exposure and safety calculations.
distractors: RHM is an output rate, not a half-life.
RHM concerns exposure rate in air, not film density.
RHM is for gamma sources; mA is an X-ray quantity.

content.stem: For direct-exposure (non-fluorescent-screen) industrial film, the reciprocity law means that:
options: The same mA-time product gives the same density regardless of how it is split
content.explanation: With direct or lead-screen film, density depends on the total exposure (intensity times time), so trading intensity for time keeps density constant; reciprocity failure is mainly a concern with fluorescent screens.
distractors: Density depends on the product of intensity and time, not time alone.
Density depends on the product, not mA alone.
Reciprocity holds well for direct/lead-screen industrial film.

content.stem: Typical acceptable radiographic density over the area of interest is commonly in the range of about:
content.explanation: Many codes require density roughly between 1.8 and 4.0 in the area of interest. The minimum varies with the code and source: some codes set it at 1.8 for X-ray and 2.0 for gamma, with the exact minimum and maximum fixed by the governing specification.
distractors: 0.1 to 0.3 is far too light for a usable industrial radiograph.
5.0 to 7.0 is generally too dark to view with standard illuminators.
Density limits are specified, not unrestricted.

content.stem: An underexposed radiograph appears:
content.explanation: Too little exposure leaves the film light (low density), lacking sufficient darkening to reveal detail.
distractors: Too dark is overexposure, the opposite condition.
Underexposure is not a correct exposure.
Underexposure does not improve sharpness.

content.stem: An overexposed radiograph appears:
content.explanation: Excessive exposure darkens the film beyond the usable range, requiring a brighter illuminator and possibly exceeding the maximum density limit.
distractors: Too light indicates underexposure, the opposite.
Overexposure does not improve sharpness.
Overexposure does not remove scatter.

content.stem: High-contrast (low-kV) techniques generally have:
options: Narrow latitude, so a smaller thickness range is well exposed at once
content.explanation: High contrast comes with narrow exposure latitude; higher kV gives lower contrast but wider latitude, covering more thickness range in one exposure.
distractors: High contrast pairs with narrow, not wide, latitude.
Contrast technique strongly affects latitude.
Low-kV and high-kV techniques give different contrast and latitude.

content.stem: Adequate contrast and definition are verified on each radiograph by:
options: The image quality indicator (IQI) sensitivity achieved
content.explanation: The visibility of the required IQI feature confirms that the radiograph has sufficient contrast and definition (sensitivity).
distractors: Cassette color does not indicate quality.
The source serial number is traceability, not a quality check.
Room temperature does not verify radiographic quality.

content.stem: Selecting a lower kV (where penetration allows) tends to:
content.explanation: Lower kV raises subject contrast and sensitivity for a given thickness, as long as it still penetrates adequately, though exposure time lengthens.
distractors: Lower kV improves, not reduces, contrast.
kV does not directly set geometric unsharpness.
Lower kV generally lengthens, not shortens, exposure.

content.stem: Density must be reasonably uniform over the area of interest so that:
options: All required thicknesses are within the acceptable density range
content.explanation: Uniform, in-range density ensures the entire region of interest is interpretable; large density variation can push parts of the image out of range.
distractors: Uniformity is about interpretability, not making the film darker.
Uniformity does not increase scatter.
Density has nothing to do with source decay rate.

content.stem: Total radiographic unsharpness combines geometric unsharpness with:
content.explanation: Overall unsharpness blends geometric unsharpness and the inherent unsharpness of the film/screen system; both must be controlled for sharp images.
distractors: Half-life is an isotope property, not an unsharpness component.
Developer pH affects processing, not the unsharpness definition.
Cassette weight is irrelevant to unsharpness.

content.stem: Projection magnification radiography (part moved away from the film) requires:
options: A very small (micro) focal spot to keep unsharpness acceptable
content.explanation: Because increasing object-to-film distance raises Ug, magnification techniques rely on a microfocus source to keep geometric unsharpness low.
distractors: A large source would create excessive unsharpness when magnifying.
A source is required to form the image.
Magnification does not require fluorescent screens.

content.stem: If part thickness increases, to maintain density the radiographer generally must:
options: Move the part away from the film
content.explanation: Thicker sections attenuate more, so exposure and/or energy must increase to keep the same density, per the exposure chart.
distractors: Decreasing exposure would underexpose the thicker section.
Thickness change requires technique adjustment.
Moving the part away worsens geometry without fixing density correctly.

content.stem: An 'exposure factor' or 'radiographic equivalence factor' helps the radiographer:
options: Adjust exposure between different materials or energies
content.explanation: Equivalence factors convert exposures between materials (or relate energies), letting a chart for one material guide exposure for another.
distractors: Dose rate is measured by survey instruments, not an exposure factor.
Film density is read by a densitometer.
Half-life is fixed by the isotope.

content.stem: A minimum source-to-film distance is often specified to:
options: Keep geometric unsharpness within acceptable limits
content.explanation: Specifying a minimum SFD (or source-to-object distance) limits Ug so the radiograph meets sharpness requirements.
distractors: Adequate distance helps control geometry, not increase scatter.
Greater distance lengthens, not shortens, exposure.
Distance does not set the kV.

content.stem: Quantum mottle (graininess from too few photons) is worsened by:
options: Very fast systems and very short exposures with few photons
content.explanation: When too few photons form the image (fast screens, very short exposures), statistical fluctuation shows as mottle; adequate photon numbers reduce it.
distractors: Slow fine-grain film reduces, not worsens, mottle.
Adequate photon numbers reduce mottle.
Lowering kV alone does not by itself cause quantum mottle.

content.stem: If a radiograph is too dark (over the maximum density), the radiographer should:
options: Reduce exposure (or raise SFD) and reshoot
content.explanation: Excess density is corrected by reducing exposure or increasing distance and retaking the radiograph so density falls within the acceptable range.
distractors: Increasing exposure would make it darker still.
An out-of-range radiograph cannot simply be accepted.
Adjusting only developer temperature does not reliably fix an over-exposure.

content.stem: The radiographic image forms because different paths through the part:
options: Transmit different amounts of radiation to the film
Change the film color chemically by contact
content.explanation: Variations in transmitted intensity, due to thickness and density along each path, create the density pattern that is the radiographic image.
distractors: Radiography uses transmitted radiation, not reflected light.
No sound is involved in image formation.
The image forms by radiation exposure, not chemical contact color change.

content.stem: Choosing kV too low for a thickness will:
options: Fail to penetrate, underexposing the image
content.explanation: If kV is below what the thickness needs, the beam cannot penetrate adequately and the image is underexposed and unusable.
distractors: Too low kV under-penetrates; it does not over-penetrate.
Inadequate penetration does not improve definition.
Low kV does not eliminate scatter.

content.stem: Higher radiographic contrast generally improves the detectability of:
options: Small differences in thickness, such as fine discontinuities
content.explanation: Greater contrast makes small attenuation differences more visible, improving sensitivity to subtle discontinuities, within the limits of latitude.
distractors: Higher contrast helps detect small as well as large features.
Contrast does affect detectability.
Contrast improves flaw detection, not scatter visibility.

content.stem: Increasing exposure (mA-time or curie-minutes) while holding geometry and energy fixed will:
content.explanation: More total exposure darkens the film, raising density, up to the limits of the film's response.
distractors: More exposure increases, not decreases, density.
Exposure strongly affects density.
Exposure does not change the set energy.

content.stem: Producing a quality radiograph requires balancing:
options: Density, contrast, definition, and acceptable distortion together
content.explanation: Quality is the combined result of adequate density, sufficient contrast and definition, and controlled distortion, all verified by the IQI.
distractors: Density alone does not ensure quality.
Contrast alone is insufficient.
Exposure time alone does not define quality.

content.stem: Image distortion (a feature appearing the wrong size or shape) is minimized by:
options: Proper alignment of source, part, and film
content.explanation: Distortion is reduced when the central beam is aligned through the area of interest and the source, part, and film are properly oriented and centered.
distractors: A larger source worsens unsharpness, not distortion control.
Greater object-to-film distance increases unsharpness and can worsen geometry.
Random tilting introduces distortion rather than reducing it.

content.stem: Which statement is correct?
options: kV sets energy/penetration; mA-time sets quantity; SFD affects intensity by inverse square; Ug = F t / d
mA sets energy; kV sets quantity
SFD has no effect on density
content.explanation: kV controls energy and penetration, mA and time control quantity, SFD affects intensity by the inverse square law, and geometric unsharpness is F t / d.
distractors: kV sets energy and mA-time sets quantity, not the reverse.
SFD strongly affects density through the inverse square law.
Geometric unsharpness is F t / d, not kV over mA.

content.stem: Exposure of radiographic film creates a:
options: Latent image in the silver halide that processing makes visible
content.explanation: Radiation alters silver halide crystals to form an invisible latent image; development converts exposed crystals to metallic silver, making the image visible.
distractors: The image is latent (invisible) until developed, not instantly visible.
The image is photographic, not magnetic.
Film records radiation exposure, not sound.

content.stem: The basic manual film processing sequence is:
content.explanation: Film is developed to form the image, stopped to halt development, fixed to remove undeveloped halide, washed to remove chemicals, and dried.
distractors: Fixing must follow development, not precede it.
Washing and drying come at the end, not the start.
This order is reversed and incorrect.

content.stem: The developer solution:
options: Reduces exposed silver halide to metallic silver, forming the image
content.explanation: The developer chemically reduces the exposed (latent-image) crystals to black metallic silver; unexposed crystals are left for the fixer to remove.
distractors: Removing unexposed halide is the fixer's job.
Stopping development is the stop bath's role.
Drying is the final step, not the developer's function.

content.stem: The fixer (hypo):
options: Removes undeveloped silver halide and makes the image permanent
content.explanation: The fixer dissolves the remaining unexposed halide so the image is stable and the clear areas stay clear; it does not develop the image.
distractors: Development is done by the developer, not the fixer.
The fixer clears unexposed halide; it does not add density.
Washing after fixing is still required to remove residual chemicals.

content.stem: The stop bath (or rinse) between developer and fixer serves to:
options: Halt development and reduce carryover into the fixer
content.explanation: The stop bath neutralizes or rinses developer, stopping development cleanly and protecting the fixer from contamination.
distractors: It stops, rather than performs, development.
It does not dry the film.
It is unrelated to scatter.

content.stem: Inadequate final washing of film leads to:
options: Residual chemicals that cause staining and poor long-term keeping
content.explanation: Leftover fixer and chemicals left by poor washing cause staining and deterioration over time, harming archival quality.
distractors: Poor washing degrades, not sharpens, the radiograph over time.
Residual chemicals do not improve contrast.
Poor washing does not aid drying and can leave residues.

content.stem: Developer temperature and development time are controlled because higher temperature:
options: Speeds development and can increase density and fog if not controlled
content.explanation: Warmer developer works faster, raising density and potentially fog; time and temperature are matched (per the processing chart) for consistent results.
distractors: Temperature strongly affects development.
Excess temperature can raise fog, harming quality.
Higher temperature speeds, not stops, development.

content.stem: Film fog (unwanted overall density) can be caused by:
options: Stray radiation, heat, age, light leaks, or over-development
content.explanation: Fog is a base density increase from stray exposure, heat, outdated film, light leaks, or excessive development; it lowers contrast.
distractors: Correct exposure forms the image, not fog.
Proper safelight use avoids fog.
Fresh, properly stored film has low fog.

content.stem: The characteristic (H&D) curve of a film plots:
options: Density versus the logarithm of exposure
content.explanation: The characteristic curve relates film density to log exposure; its slope (gradient) indicates film contrast at a given density.
distractors: Dose versus distance is an inverse-square plot, not the characteristic curve.
kV versus mA is not the characteristic curve.
Time versus temperature is a processing chart, not the H&D curve.

content.stem: The gradient (slope) of the characteristic curve represents the film's:
content.explanation: A steeper gradient means higher film contrast at that density; the curve also conveys speed and latitude information.
distractors: Speed relates to horizontal position of the curve, not its slope alone.
Granularity is a separate noise characteristic.
Fog is the base density, not the gradient.

content.stem: Automatic film processors improve consistency by:
options: Controlling time, temperature, replenishment, and transport
content.explanation: Automatic processors hold development time and temperature constant, replenish chemistry, and transport film through develop, fix, wash, and dry stages for repeatable results.
distractors: Fixing is still performed in automatic processors.
Washing is still part of automatic processing.
Automatic processors use processing chemicals.

content.stem: Chemical replenishment in processing maintains:
options: Consistent developer and fixer activity as solutions are used
content.explanation: As chemicals are depleted, replenishment restores their strength so density and contrast stay consistent across many films.
distractors: kV is an exposure parameter, not affected by replenishment.
Source activity decays by half-life, unrelated to replenishment.
Film grain is a manufacturing property, not set by replenishment.

content.stem: A darkroom safelight must be:
options: A color and intensity that will not fog the film at the working distance
content.explanation: Safelights use a filtered color and low intensity to which the film is relatively insensitive, allowing handling without fogging.
distractors: Bright white light would fog the film.
Ultraviolet would expose/fog the film.
Safelights are specifically filtered to the safe color.

content.stem: Crescent-shaped marks on a radiograph are usually caused by:
