options: Kinking or bending the film during handling
content.explanation: Bending or crimping the film before processing creates crescent (half-moon) artifacts; careful handling prevents them.
distractors: Correct exposure does not create crescent marks.
Proper washing does not cause artifacts.
Good contact prevents blur, not crescent marks (which come from handling).

content.stem: Branched or tree-like dark marks on film are typically:
content.explanation: Static discharge during rapid film handling in dry conditions creates branching marks; controlling humidity and handling reduces them.
distractors: These are film artifacts, not part cracks.
They are not porosity in the part.
They are artifacts, not genuine discontinuity indications.

content.stem: Water spots or drying marks on a radiograph result from:
options: Uneven drying or contaminated wash water
content.explanation: Droplets and contaminants left during drying leave spots; a wetting agent and clean water with even drying prevent them.
distractors: Correct processing avoids such marks.
IQI placement is unrelated to drying spots.
kV does not cause drying spots.

content.stem: Pressure or scratch marks on film appear when:
options: Film is roughly handled or scratched before processing
content.explanation: Mechanical pressure or scratching of the emulsion creates artifacts; gentle handling and clean equipment prevent them.
distractors: Source decay is unrelated to handling marks.
Correct kV does not cause handling marks.
Uniform density is a goal, not a cause of marks.

content.stem: Distinguishing a film artifact from a real discontinuity often requires:
options: Checking both films/sides and reprocessing or re-shooting if in doubt
content.explanation: Artifacts can be confirmed by examining the emulsion surfaces, comparing films, or retaking the radiograph; genuine indications persist as true density changes in the image.
distractors: Ignoring a suspect mark risks misinterpretation.
Rejecting without confirming the cause may scrap good parts.
Raising kV does not resolve whether a mark is an artifact.

content.stem: For archival storage, processed radiographs must be:
options: Thoroughly washed and dried, then stored cool, dry, and protected
content.explanation: Proper washing removes residual chemicals, and cool, dry, protected storage preserves the image for the required retention period.
distractors: Wet storage promotes deterioration.
Film cannot be left in fixer for storage.
Light exposure can damage stored radiographs.

content.stem: Radiographs should be interpreted:
options: On a suitable illuminator in subdued ambient light with masking of bright areas
content.explanation: Interpretation uses a high-intensity illuminator in a darkened room, masking bright surrounds and glare so subtle density changes are visible.
distractors: Bright sunlight prevents seeing subtle density changes.
Some controlled light is required to view the film.
A densitometer measures spots; interpretation needs full-film viewing on an illuminator.

content.stem: Film density required by the code is verified using a:
options: Densitometer (often referenced to a calibrated step strip)
content.explanation: A calibrated densitometer reads the optical density to confirm it meets the specified range.
distractors: A survey meter measures radiation, not density.
A pocket dosimeter measures personnel dose.
A refractometer measures liquid concentration, not film density.

content.stem: Exhausted or contaminated developer typically produces radiographs that are:
content.explanation: Weak developer fails to build adequate density and contrast; this is corrected by replenishment or fresh chemistry.
distractors: Exhausted developer underdevelops, giving light, not dark, films.
It does not improve sharpness.
Poor chemistry can increase, not remove, fog or other defects.

content.stem: Films are dried after washing to:
options: Make them ready for handling, viewing, and storage without damage
content.explanation: Drying completes processing so films can be handled and stored; it neither develops nor changes the recorded image.
distractors: Development occurs earlier, not during drying.
Drying does not add density.
Drying does not remove the image.

content.stem: Fog reduces radiographic quality mainly by:
options: Lowering contrast (reducing the visibility of small density differences)
content.explanation: A raised base density from fog compresses the usable density range, lowering contrast and the ability to see fine detail.
distractors: Fog does not increase sharpness.
Fog degrades, not improves, sensitivity.
Fog is unrelated to penetration.

content.stem: In digital radiography, image quality is described partly by:
content.explanation: Digital image quality depends on signal-to-noise ratio, contrast sensitivity, and spatial resolution, replacing film-specific measures.
distractors: Developer temperature is a film-processing parameter.
Fixer pH is a film-processing parameter.
Digital systems have no film grain.

content.stem: Contrast sensitivity in digital radiography refers to:
options: The smallest thickness/attenuation change the system can reveal
content.explanation: Contrast sensitivity expresses the smallest attenuation difference detectable, analogous to the role of contrast and IQI sensitivity in film radiography.
distractors: Pixel count relates to spatial resolution, not contrast sensitivity alone.
Cassette color is irrelevant.
Half-life is a source property, not an image-quality measure.

content.stem: A processing control strip is used to:
options: Monitor processor performance (density steps) over time
content.explanation: Control strips with known step densities are processed regularly to detect drift in processor chemistry, temperature, or timing.
distractors: Control strips do not measure dose.
They do not shield film.
They do not set exposure kV.

content.stem: Loading two films of different speeds in one cassette (double loading) allows:
options: Capturing a wider thickness range in a single exposure
content.explanation: A faster and a slower film together cover a broader density/thickness range from one exposure, useful for parts with thickness variation.
distractors: An IQI is still required on each technique.
Both films still require processing.
Double loading does not remove scatter.

content.stem: Clean, dry hands and clean work surfaces in the darkroom prevent:
options: Fingerprints, chemical spots, and contamination artifacts on film
content.explanation: Contamination from hands or surfaces leaves marks on the emulsion; cleanliness prevents these artifacts.
distractors: Cleanliness supports, not prevents, correct results.
Cleanliness does not impede development.
Source decay is unrelated to darkroom cleanliness.

content.stem: Fixing time is commonly set to about twice the:
options: Clearing time (time for the film to clear)
content.explanation: A common rule fixes film for roughly twice the clearing time to ensure complete removal of unexposed halide.
distractors: Fixing time is referenced to clearing time, not development time.
Wash time is a separate step.
Exposure time is unrelated to fixing duration.

content.stem: Over-development of film tends to increase:
options: Density and fog, reducing usable contrast
content.explanation: Developing too long or too warm raises overall density and fog, compressing contrast and degrading quality.
distractors: Over-development does not improve sharpness.
Development does not change beam penetration.
It has no effect on source activity.

content.stem: Spots or marks reproduced identically on many radiographs point to:
options: A defect in a reused screen or processor, not the part
content.explanation: An artifact appearing in the same place on many films indicates a screen or processor defect rather than a genuine, part-specific discontinuity.
distractors: Identical repeated marks are not a per-part flaw.
Repeated artifacts indicate a problem, not correct technique.
A consistently repeated mark is not random noise.

content.stem: Base-plus-fog density is the density of:
options: The densest part of the image
content.explanation: Base-plus-fog is the minimum density of processed but unexposed film; excessive base-plus-fog signals film or processing problems.
distractors: A fully exposed film has high density, not base-plus-fog.
The densest image area is not base-plus-fog.
The IQI is an image-quality device, not a density baseline.

content.stem: A wetting agent in the final rinse helps:
options: Even drying and prevention of water spots
content.explanation: A wetting agent reduces surface tension so water sheets off evenly, preventing drying spots.
distractors: It does not develop the image.
It does not affect contrast.
It does not remove the image.

content.stem: Digital image post-processing (windowing, contrast adjustment) must be:
options: Controlled per procedure so it does not mask or create indications
content.explanation: Digital enhancement is allowed within qualified limits; uncontrolled adjustment could obscure real flaws or create false ones, so it follows procedure.
distractors: Arbitrary adjustment risks misinterpretation.
Controlled post-processing is a benefit of digital systems, not to be avoided.
Post-processing must never be used to hide flaws.

content.stem: A time-temperature processing chart is used to:
options: Select development time for the developer temperature
content.explanation: Because warmer developer works faster, the chart pairs the correct development time with the measured temperature for consistent density.
distractors: The chart does not set kV.
It does not select the radiation source.
It does not measure dose.

content.stem: Most film-handling artifacts are prevented by:
options: Careful, clean handling and proper darkroom conditions
content.explanation: Crescent, static, pressure, and contamination marks are avoided by gentle, clean handling and controlled humidity and lighting.
distractors: kV does not address handling artifacts.
SFD is a geometry factor, not a handling-artifact control.
Scatter is unrelated to handling artifacts and is itself undesirable.

content.stem: Whether a finished radiograph is acceptable for interpretation is judged by:
options: Density, IQI sensitivity, and freedom from masking artifacts
content.explanation: Acceptability requires in-range density, the required IQI sensitivity, and no artifacts that could mask or mimic discontinuities.
distractors: Film brand alone does not determine acceptability.
Exposure time alone is insufficient.
The source serial number is traceability, not an acceptance check.

content.stem: A practical advantage of digital detectors is their wide dynamic range, which:
options: Can capture a broad thickness range in one exposure with post-processing
Removes the need for an IQI
content.explanation: Wide dynamic range lets one digital exposure cover varied thickness, with windowing to view different ranges, though an IQI is still required.
distractors: Digital methods still use radiation.
An IQI is still required to demonstrate quality.
Digital images can still contain artifacts.

content.stem: Which processing order and purpose pairing is correct?
options: Developer forms image; stop halts development; fixer clears unexposed halide; wash removes chemicals; dry finishes
Fixer forms image; developer clears halide
content.explanation: Developer forms the image, the stop bath halts development, the fixer clears unexposed halide, washing removes residual chemicals, and drying finishes the film.
distractors: The developer forms the image and the fixer clears halide, not the reverse.
Washing removes chemicals; it does not develop the image.
Drying finishes the film; it does not form the image.

content.stem: The purpose of an image quality indicator (IQI / penetrameter) is to:
content.explanation: An IQI provides a known reference whose visibility on the radiograph shows that the technique achieved the required sensitivity; it does not measure flaw size directly.
distractors: An IQI indicates technique quality, not the part's thickness.
An IQI is imaged, not used as shielding.
An IQI does not develop the image.

content.stem: A hole-type (plaque) IQI has holes commonly designated:
options: 1T, 2T, and 4T relative to the IQI thickness
content.explanation: Hole-type IQIs carry 1T, 2T, and 4T holes (multiples of the plaque thickness T), and the IQI thickness is a percentage of the part thickness.
distractors: A, B, C designate wire IQI sets, not plaque holes.
X, Y, Z are not standard IQI hole designations.
Colors are not IQI hole designations.

content.stem: A wire-type IQI consists of:
options: A set of wires of graduated diameters
content.explanation: Wire IQIs are sets of parallel wires of increasing diameter; the thinnest wire visible indicates the sensitivity achieved.
distractors: A holed plate is the hole-type IQI, a different design.
A lead letter is an identification marker, not an IQI.
A plastic step wedge is a calibration aid, not a wire IQI.

content.stem: A '2-2T' radiographic quality level means:
options: IQI thickness 2 percent of part thickness with the 2T hole visible
content.explanation: In 2-2T, the plaque IQI is 2 percent of the specimen thickness and the 2T hole (diameter twice the plaque thickness) must be visible, a common required sensitivity level.
distractors: It is a percent-thickness and hole designation, not a physical 2-inch size.
It is not an exposure setting.
It refers to a hole-type IQI, not wire diameters.

content.stem: Higher radiographic sensitivity (for example 1-1T versus 2-2T) means the technique can reveal:
content.explanation: A more demanding IQI level (thinner plaque, smaller hole, or thinner wire visible) indicates the technique resolves smaller attenuation differences, i.e. higher sensitivity.
distractors: Higher sensitivity reveals smaller, not only larger, features.
Sensitivity is about detail resolved, not part thickness limits.
Higher sensitivity shows more, not less, detail.

content.stem: IQIs are normally placed on the:
options: Source side of the part, when accessible
content.explanation: Source-side placement is standard because it represents the least favorable position; film-side placement is allowed only when source-side is inaccessible and must be marked.
distractors: Film-side placement is the exception, not the default, and is marked.
The IQI sits on the part, not inside the cassette.
The IQI is not placed on the densitometer.

content.stem: When an IQI must be placed on the film side, the radiograph must:
options: Carry a lead letter 'F' to show film-side placement
Have the IQI removed from the image
content.explanation: Film-side IQI placement is identified by a lead 'F' so the interpreter knows the sensitivity was demonstrated under the more favorable film-side condition.
distractors: Film-side placement is permitted when necessary, not an automatic reject.
An IQI is still required.
The IQI must remain imaged for verification.

content.stem: The IQI material should be:
options: Radiographically similar to the part material
content.explanation: IQIs are made of a material radiographically similar to the part (same group) so the demonstrated sensitivity applies to that material.
distractors: Lead is too different in attenuation to represent most parts.
Aluminum suits aluminum parts but not steel; the IQI must match the part group.
Plastic does not represent metal parts radiographically.

content.stem: The 'essential hole' or 'essential wire' is the:
options: Specific IQI feature required to be visible for the technique to qualify
content.explanation: The essential hole (plaque) or essential wire (wire IQI) is the designated feature that must be visible to meet the required sensitivity level.
distractors: It is the required feature for the level, not simply the largest hole.
It is not the identification number.
It is not the backscatter 'B' letter.

content.stem: Equivalent penetrameter sensitivity (EPS) is used to:
options: Compare or convert sensitivity between different IQI types or placements
content.explanation: EPS expresses the sensitivity in a common way so requirements can be met by an equivalent IQI when the exact specified one is impractical.
distractors: EPS is a sensitivity concept, not a dose measurement.
It does not set processing time.
It is unrelated to shielding.

content.stem: A shim of similar material is sometimes placed under a hole-type IQI on a weld to:
options: Account for weld reinforcement thickness so the IQI represents the correct thickness
content.explanation: On welds, a shim raises the effective thickness under the IQI to match the weld plus reinforcement, so the IQI represents the section being examined.
distractors: The shim is for thickness representation, not to increase scatter.
It is not a shield.
It does not process film.

content.stem: A single-wall single-image (SWSI) technique exposes:
options: One wall, with the IQI and image representing that wall
content.explanation: In SWSI the beam passes through and images a single wall, used when the source can be placed inside or with access to one wall at a time.
distractors: Superimposing both walls is a double-wall technique.
The elliptical double image is a small-diameter pipe technique, not SWSI.
SWSI images one wall, not none.

content.stem: A double-wall single-image (DWSI) technique is used when:
options: The beam passes through both walls but only the far wall is interpreted
content.explanation: DWSI passes through both walls of a pipe but the film-side (far) wall is the one interpreted; it suits diameters too large for the elliptical technique with limited access.
distractors: Double-wall techniques apply to pipe with two walls.
DWSI is used with external source placement, not always internal.
An IQI is still required.

content.stem: The double-wall double-image (elliptical) technique is typically used on:
options: Small-diameter pipe, imaging both walls as an offset ellipse
content.explanation: For small-diameter pipe, offsetting the beam projects the near and far weld as an ellipse so both walls are interpreted in one image, usually requiring two exposures 90 degrees apart.
distractors: Thick plate uses single-wall techniques.
Large vessels use single-wall or DWSI approaches, not the elliptical method.
Solid bar is not a pipe-weld geometry.

content.stem: A panoramic exposure with the source inside a pipe:
options: Images the full circumferential weld in one exposure
content.explanation: A source centered in the pipe with film wrapped outside exposes the entire circumferential weld at once, the most efficient technique when internal access exists.
distractors: Panoramic exposure replaces many separate shots with one.
It is specifically used to image circumferential welds.
A source is required.

content.stem: Lead location markers placed on the part:
options: Provide traceable reference points to relocate any indication on the part
content.explanation: Location markers appear on the film and on the part so an indication's position can be reliably found on the actual part for evaluation or repair.
distractors: Markers do not measure dose.
They do not shield the IQI.
They do not process film.

content.stem: When multiple exposures cover a long weld, adjacent films should:
options: Overlap so no length is left unexamined
content.explanation: Overlapping coverage ensures the entire weld length is radiographed with no unexamined gaps, with location markers tying films to positions.
distractors: Gaps would leave weld length unexamined.
Adjacent films image different positions, not identical content.
Location markers are needed to index the films.

content.stem: The number of exposures needed around a circumferential weld depends on:
options: Diameter, thickness, source-to-film geometry, and the required coverage/sensitivity
content.explanation: Geometry (diameter, wall thickness, SFD) and the required coverage and sensitivity determine how many exposures are needed to image the whole weld acceptably.
distractors: Film color is irrelevant.
Developer brand does not set exposure count.
Operator height is irrelevant.

content.stem: Each radiograph must carry identification that:
options: Uniquely traces it to the part, weld, and location
content.explanation: Permanent identification (part, weld, location, and date as required) provides traceability and must be present on the radiograph.
distractors: Identification is required, not optional.
It must identify the part and location, not only the date.
Identification is set up before exposure for traceability, not added later.

content.stem: An IQI should be placed:
options: In the area of interest representing the thickness being examined
content.explanation: The IQI represents the section under examination, so it is placed in or adjacent to the area of interest at a representative thickness.
distractors: It must represent the examined thickness, not an unrelated thick section.
It must be within the imaged area to appear on the film.
The IQI is not placed on the source.

content.stem: Wire IQI sets (A, B, C, D) differ by:
options: The range of wire diameters they contain
content.explanation: Each wire IQI set covers a different range of wire diameters; the set is selected so the essential wire falls in a usable range for the part thickness.
distractors: The sets are distinguished by wire size range, not color.
They have no developer requirement of their own.
Wire sets have no half-life.

content.stem: Demonstrating 2-2T sensitivity means the technique can show a thickness change of about:
content.explanation: Roughly, the 2 percent IQI level corresponds to detecting a thickness change near 2 percent of the part thickness, though IQI sensitivity is a technique indicator rather than a direct flaw-size guarantee.
distractors: It is a percentage of thickness, not a fixed 2 inches.
It refers to specimen thickness, not source size.
It is about 2 percent, not 20 percent.

content.stem: Source-side IQI placement is preferred because the source side is the:
options: Less favorable position, giving a conservative sensitivity demonstration
content.explanation: Radiation quality and unsharpness are least favorable on the source side, so demonstrating sensitivity there conservatively covers the whole thickness.
distractors: Source side is the less, not more, favorable position.
Source and film sides are not radiographically the same.
It is a deliberate conservative choice, not merely where it fits.

content.stem: Choosing between single-wall and double-wall techniques depends mainly on:
options: Pipe diameter and the access available to the source and film
content.explanation: Geometry and access drive the choice: internal access allows single-wall/panoramic, while limited access on small pipe leads to double-wall techniques.
distractors: Film color does not drive technique selection.
Developer temperature is a processing parameter.
Selection is governed by geometry and code, not preference alone.

content.stem: Confirming that the required weld length and thickness were covered relies on:
options: Location markers and overlap on the radiographs
content.explanation: Location markers and overlapping films demonstrate complete coverage of the weld; density and IQI confirm quality within each film.
distractors: A densitometer checks density, not coverage extent.
A survey meter measures radiation, not coverage.
The source serial number is traceability, not coverage.

content.stem: An IQI demonstrates technique sensitivity but does NOT:
options: Directly measure the size of an actual discontinuity
content.explanation: The IQI confirms the radiograph's quality level; actual discontinuities are sized by other means (scales, comparison) per the procedure, not read off the IQI.
distractors: Indicating image quality is exactly what the IQI does.
Showing the required sensitivity is the IQI's purpose.
Confirming contrast and definition is part of its role.

content.stem: On a long radiograph with varying thickness, codes may require:
options: More than one IQI to represent the range of thicknesses
content.explanation: When thickness varies across the film, multiple IQIs may be required so sensitivity is demonstrated across the represented thickness range.
distractors: An IQI is always required.
Source-side placement is preferred where accessible, not film side by default.
The IQI goes on the part, not the densitometer.

content.stem: Hole-type and wire-type IQIs:
options: Are alternative IQI designs, selected per the governing code
content.explanation: Both designs indicate technique sensitivity; the governing code or contract specifies which type and level applies.
distractors: Both indicate sensitivity, just by different features.
They are different designs, not identical.
Neither is a dosimeter.

content.stem: The elliptical (DWDI) technique on small pipe typically requires:
options: Two exposures about 90 degrees apart to cover the full weld
content.explanation: Because each elliptical exposure clearly images only part of the circumference, two shots roughly 90 degrees apart are used to cover the whole weld.
distractors: A single elliptical exposure does not adequately cover the full circumference.
Location markers are still required.
DWDI uses an external source, not a panoramic internal source.

content.stem: Adequate source-to-object distance in pipe radiography helps ensure:
options: Acceptable geometric unsharpness and weld coverage per the technique
content.explanation: Sufficient distance controls geometric unsharpness and the projected coverage geometry; it generally lengthens exposure, and an IQI is still required.
distractors: Proper distance does not increase fog.
Greater distance lengthens, not shortens, exposure.
An IQI is always required.

content.stem: Location markers should be placed on the part such that:
options: Their position on the film unambiguously locates indications on the part
They never appear on the film
content.explanation: Markers are positioned (and their source/film side noted where relevant) so any indication on the film can be traced to the exact spot on the part.
distractors: Markers must appear on the film to be useful.
Markers must not obscure the weld.
Markers do not replace the IQI.

content.stem: If the required IQI level is not visible, the radiographer should:
options: Adjust technique (energy, exposure, geometry, scatter control) and reshoot
content.explanation: Failure to show the essential IQI feature means the technique did not meet sensitivity; the radiographer corrects the technique and retakes the radiograph.
distractors: An insufficient-sensitivity radiograph cannot be accepted.
The IQI must remain imaged.
Ambient light is a viewing condition, not a fix for technique sensitivity.

content.stem: Without a shim under the IQI on a weld with reinforcement, the IQI may:
options: Represent less than the actual examined thickness, overstating sensitivity
content.explanation: If the IQI sits on base metal thinner than the weld plus reinforcement, it represents less thickness and can overstate the achieved sensitivity, so a shim is used.
distractors: Without a shim it represents less, not more, thickness.
It does affect how sensitivity is represented.
An IQI is not a dosimeter.

content.stem: The radiographic technique (energy, SFD, IQI, geometry) should be:
options: Documented so the examination is repeatable and traceable
content.explanation: Recording the technique parameters ensures repeatability, traceability, and review against the procedure and code.
distractors: Relying on memory is not acceptable documentation.
Random changes undermine repeatability.
Technique records support, not avoid, review.

content.stem: For a hole-type IQI, the plaque thickness is normally a small percentage of the:
content.explanation: The plaque is a defined percentage (commonly about 2 percent) of the part thickness, so the IQI scales with the section examined.
distractors: It scales with part thickness, not source size.
It is not based on film thickness.
It is unrelated to developer volume.

content.stem: For a hole-type IQI to be valid, the interpreter must be able to see:
options: The IQI outline and the essential hole
content.explanation: The IQI body and the required (essential) hole must be visible on the radiograph to confirm the sensitivity level was met.
distractors: The identification numbers alone do not demonstrate the hole sensitivity.
The part edge is not the sensitivity indicator.
A survey meter is unrelated to film interpretation.

content.stem: In the elliptical technique, offsetting the beam is done to:
options: Separate the near and far weld images so both can be interpreted
content.explanation: Beam offset projects the top and bottom of the weld as a separated ellipse so the two walls do not superimpose and each can be evaluated.
distractors: The offset is for image separation, not to increase scatter.
It does not shorten exposure.
An IQI is still required.

content.stem: Which technique suits a large-diameter pipe with internal source access?
content.explanation: With internal access on a large pipe, a panoramic single-wall exposure images the full weld efficiently in one shot.
distractors: The elliptical technique is for small-diameter pipe.
DWSI from outside is used when internal access is unavailable.
Radiography is possible with appropriate technique.

content.stem: Wire IQIs are oriented so the wires:
options: Lie across the weld/area of interest as required by the code
content.explanation: Wire IQIs are placed with the wires positioned (often across the weld) per the code so the essential wire's visibility validly demonstrates sensitivity.
distractors: Orientation follows the code relative to the weld, not the source cable.
The IQI must be visible, not hidden behind lead.
Orientation has nothing to do with a survey meter.

content.stem: Which statement about IQIs is correct?
options: They demonstrate technique sensitivity and are normally placed source-side in the area of interest
They are placed only on the film side
content.explanation: IQIs show the technique met the required sensitivity and are normally placed on the source side within the area of interest; film-side placement is the marked exception.
distractors: IQIs do not directly measure flaw depth.
Source-side is the default; film-side is the exception.
IQIs are not dosimeters.

content.stem: On a radiograph, a discontinuity that removes material (such as a void) appears:
options: Darker than the surrounding sound metal
The same density as the metal
content.explanation: Less material in the path lets more radiation through, darkening that area of the film; voids, porosity, and most volumetric flaws image as darker spots.
distractors: Lighter areas correspond to more material or denser inclusions, not voids.
A void changes local density, so it differs from sound metal.
Adequate technique makes such discontinuities visible.

content.stem: A high-density inclusion such as tungsten in a weld appears on film as:
content.explanation: A tungsten inclusion absorbs more radiation than the surrounding metal, so less reaches the film and the spot images lighter.
distractors: Darker areas indicate less material; a dense inclusion does the opposite.
A dense inclusion does produce an indication.
It is a rounded dense indication, not a crack.

content.stem: Gas porosity in a weld typically appears as:
options: Rounded dark spots, individually or in clusters
content.explanation: Gas pockets are voids, imaging as rounded dark indications that may be scattered, clustered, or aligned depending on how the gas was trapped.
distractors: Porosity is rounded and dark, not light straight lines.
Porosity is localized, not a uniform band.
Porosity produces visible dark indications.

content.stem: Slag inclusions in a weld usually appear as:
options: Dark irregular shapes, sometimes elongated along the weld
A light line at the root
content.explanation: Trapped slag is less dense than the weld metal, imaging as dark, irregular, often elongated indications, frequently between passes or at the sidewall.
distractors: Slag is dark and irregular, not bright rounded dots (which suggest dense inclusions).
A light root line suggests a dense feature, not slag.
Slag produces visible dark indications.

content.stem: Lack of fusion (LOF) often appears on a radiograph as:
options: A dark line, sometimes straight, at the weld interface or between passes
content.explanation: LOF is an unbonded interface; when favorably oriented it images as a dark line at the fusion face or between passes, though it can be hard to detect if tightly closed.
distractors: LOF images dark, not bright.
LOF is typically linear, not solely a rounded void.
LOF produces a local density change, not uniform density.

content.stem: Incomplete (lack of) penetration in a groove weld typically appears as:
options: A straight dark line at the weld root
content.explanation: When the root is not filled, the gap images as a relatively straight dark line along the root, often with fairly defined edges.
distractors: It is dark, not bright.
It is a linear root indication, not scattered light dots.
It produces a visible indication.

content.stem: Cracks are most readily detected by radiography when they are:
options: Favorably oriented (roughly parallel to the beam)
content.explanation: A crack must present enough through-thickness gap along the beam to image as a dark line; tight cracks across the beam can be missed, which is a known RT limitation versus surface methods.
distractors: Cracks across the beam present little path difference and are easily missed.
Detection strongly depends on orientation.
Cracks are detectable as voids, not only when slag-filled.

content.stem: Undercut at the weld toe appears on a radiograph as:
options: A dark irregular line along the edge of the weld
content.explanation: Undercut is a groove melted into the base metal at the weld toe; the reduced thickness images as a darker irregular band along the weld edge.
distractors: Undercut is dark, not bright, and lies at the toe, not center.
Undercut is linear at the edge, not rounded dense spots.
It is a localized dark indication, not a uniform light area.

content.stem: Burn-through (excess root melting) tends to appear as:
options: A localized dark area at the root where metal was lost
content.explanation: Burn-through removes or sags root metal, imaging as a darker localized region at the root, often with surrounding contour changes.
distractors: Lost metal images darker, not brighter.
It is a localized area, not solely a fine straight line.
It produces a visible indication.

content.stem: Excessive weld reinforcement appears on a radiograph as:
options: A lighter band over the weld due to the added thickness
content.explanation: Added reinforcement is extra material, so that band images lighter than the adjacent base metal; it is a contour condition, not a subsurface flaw.
distractors: Added material images lighter, not as a dark void.
Reinforcement is added metal, not a crack.
It is a thickness condition, not porosity.

content.stem: Root concavity (suck-back) typically images as:
options: A darker band along the weld centerline at the root
content.explanation: Concavity at the root reduces thickness along the centerline, imaging as a darker band there; its smooth contour distinguishes it from a crack.
distractors: Reduced thickness images darker, not brighter.
It is a contour loss, not dense inclusions.
Reduced thickness does change density.

content.stem: Tungsten inclusions are associated with which welding process?
content.explanation: Tungsten inclusions occur when the GTAW electrode contacts the weld pool, leaving dense tungsten particles that image as light spots.
distractors: Oxyacetylene welding does not use a tungsten electrode.
Brazing does not introduce tungsten electrode particles.
Riveting is not a welding/fusion process.

content.stem: A localized group of rounded dark indications is best described as:
content.explanation: Several rounded gas voids grouped together are cluster porosity; the rounded, grouped appearance distinguishes it from linear flaws.
distractors: A crack is linear, not a cluster of rounded spots.
Lack of penetration is a linear root indication.
Undercut is a linear edge indication.

content.stem: Continuous or intermittent dark lines paralleling the weld, located between passes or at the sidewall, most likely indicate:
content.explanation: Parallel dark lines along the weld, often called wagon tracks, are elongated slag trapped along pass boundaries or sidewalls.
distractors: Tungsten inclusions image as light, rounded dense spots.
Excess reinforcement images lighter, not as dark lines.
Root concavity is a centerline contour, not parallel sidewall lines.

content.stem: In castings, gas porosity appears on a radiograph as:
options: Rounded dark spots, sometimes with smooth edges
content.explanation: Gas trapped during solidification leaves rounded voids that image as dark spots, similar in character to weld porosity.
distractors: Gas porosity is a void (dark), not a dense light spot.
Porosity is rounded, not straight light lines.
It produces visible dark indications.

content.stem: Shrinkage in castings often appears as:
content.explanation: Shrinkage forms where metal contracts on cooling, imaging as dark, irregular, sometimes branching or sponge-like indications, often at thick sections or junctions.
distractors: Shrinkage images dark, not as bright dense dots.
It is irregular/branching, not a single light line.
It produces local density changes, not uniform density.

content.stem: A cold shut in a casting is:
options: A dark line where two metal streams failed to fuse
content.explanation: A cold shut occurs when metal flows meet without fusing; the unbonded boundary images as a dark line, often smooth and curved.
distractors: A cold shut is an unfused boundary (dark), not a dense inclusion.
It is a fusion defect, not excess thickness.
It is a subsurface fusion line, not merely a surface scratch.

content.stem: Hot tears in castings typically appear as:
options: Ragged dark lines, often branching, near restrained thick sections
content.explanation: Hot tears form from stresses while the casting is still hot, imaging as ragged, often branching dark cracks, commonly where contraction is restrained.
distractors: Hot tears are dark and ragged, not smooth and bright.
They are linear/branching, not rounded dense spots.
They are localized cracks, not uniform bands.

content.stem: Sand or oxide inclusions in a casting generally appear as:
options: Dark irregular indications (less dense than the metal)
content.explanation: Most nonmetallic inclusions are less dense than the casting metal, imaging as dark irregular spots; unusually dense inclusions (like chaplets) can image lighter.
distractors: Typical sand/oxide inclusions are less dense, imaging dark, not light.
They are irregular, not straight light lines.
They produce visible indications.

content.stem: A misrun (incomplete fill) in a casting appears as:
options: A dark region where metal failed to fill the mold
content.explanation: Where the mold did not fill, the missing or thin metal images as a darker area, often at extremities or thin sections of the casting.
distractors: Missing metal images darker, not as a dense bright area.
A misrun is a fill defect, not specifically a root crack.
It is a fill defect, distinct from porosity.

content.stem: Classifying an indication as linear or rounded is important because:
options: Acceptance criteria often treat linear and rounded indications differently
content.explanation: Codes commonly apply different limits to linear indications (like cracks, LOF) than to rounded ones (like porosity), so classification drives evaluation.
distractors: Classification is interpretation, not a change in film density.
It does not set exposure kV.
It does not measure dose.

content.stem: In radiography, 'interpretation' refers to identifying indications, while 'evaluation' refers to:
options: Judging them against the acceptance criteria
content.explanation: Interpretation determines what an indication is; evaluation compares it to the acceptance standard to decide accept or reject.
distractors: Film development is processing, not evaluation.
Setting exposure is technique, not evaluation.
Calibrating a densitometer is equipment control, not evaluation.

content.stem: A non-relevant indication is one that:
options: Arises from part geometry or technique, not a true discontinuity
content.explanation: Non-relevant indications come from geometry, contour, or technique rather than actual flaws; they are recognized and set aside so real discontinuities are evaluated.
distractors: Non-relevant indications are not rejectable flaws.
They are by definition not true discontinuities like cracks.
They are visible on film but not caused by a flaw.

content.stem: Before interpreting indications, the radiographer must first confirm the radiograph:
options: Meets density, IQI sensitivity, and is free of masking artifacts
Shows the source serial number only
content.explanation: A radiograph must be valid (proper density, required IQI sensitivity, no disqualifying artifacts) before any indication can be reliably interpreted.
distractors: Maximum darkness is not the validity criterion; density must be in range.
The serial number alone does not validate quality.
Speed of exposure does not establish validity.

content.stem: A surface scratch and a subsurface crack can sometimes be distinguished by:
options: Surface examination of the part and the indication's behavior on multiple views
content.explanation: Correlating the radiographic indication with surface inspection and additional views or methods helps separate a harmless surface mark from a genuine crack.
distractors: Film color does not distinguish flaw type.
Developer brand is irrelevant to interpretation.
Half-life is a source property, not an interpretation aid.

content.stem: A fundamental limitation of radiography for planar flaws is that:
options: Tight cracks not aligned with the beam may not be detected
content.explanation: RT depends on a through-thickness path difference, so tightly closed planar flaws across the beam can be missed, a key reason RT and UT/surface methods complement each other.
distractors: Not all cracks are reliably found; orientation matters.
Porosity is readily detected by RT.
Density is central to detectability.

content.stem: Excess root penetration (icicles or root sag) appears as:
options: A lighter localized area at the root from added metal
content.explanation: Extra metal protruding at the root adds thickness, imaging as a lighter localized area along the root, a contour condition rather than a void.
distractors: Added metal images lighter, not as a dark void.
It is added metal, not a crack.
Undercut is a loss of metal at the toe, the opposite condition.

content.stem: Reading the relative depth of a volumetric flaw can be aided by:
options: Comparing the indication's density to the surrounding density
content.explanation: A darker indication generally means more material was missing along that path; relative density helps estimate the flaw's extent through the thickness, within technique limits.
distractors: Radiographs are read by density, not color.
Film brand does not indicate flaw depth.
Room temperature is unrelated to interpretation.

content.stem: Acceptance criteria for the same indication type can differ between welds and castings because:
options: Different codes and service requirements apply to each product form
content.explanation: Welds and castings are governed by different standards and service expectations, so the same flaw type may have different limits in each.
distractors: Film response is not what sets acceptance criteria.
Radiation physics is the same; the codes differ.
The densitometer is not the reason criteria differ.

content.stem: Rounded indications arranged in a line along the weld are reported as:
options: Aligned (linear) porosity, which some codes treat more strictly
content.explanation: When rounded pores align, some codes treat the alignment more strictly than scattered porosity because it can indicate a planar weakness path.
distractors: Aligned rounded pores are porosity, not a single crack.
It is a void condition, not added reinforcement.
Aligned porosity is relevant and must be evaluated.

content.stem: Reliable interpretation requires viewing the radiograph:
options: On an adequate illuminator in controlled lighting by a qualified interpreter
content.explanation: Qualified interpretation uses a proper high-intensity illuminator in subdued light, with the radiograph meeting density and quality requirements.
distractors: Bright sunlight prevents seeing subtle density differences.
Density requirements are part of a valid radiograph.
Casual viewing on an uncontrolled screen is not acceptable interpretation.

content.stem: An indication appearing in the same location on multiple parts most likely is:
options: A screen or processing artifact, not a real flaw
content.explanation: A repeating, identically located mark points to a screen or processor defect rather than a genuine, part-specific discontinuity, and must be investigated before evaluation.
distractors: It is unlikely every part has a crack in the identical spot.
Repeating identical marks are not genuine per-part porosity.
An artifact is not evaluated as a rejectable flaw.

content.stem: When reporting radiographic results, the interpreter records:
options: The indication type, location, size, and accept/reject per the criteria
content.explanation: A complete report identifies each relevant indication's type, location, and extent and states the disposition against the acceptance standard.
distractors: A film count alone is not a result report.
The kV alone is technique data, not the interpretation result.
The operator name alone is not the result.

content.stem: Compared with rounded (volumetric) flaws, planar flaws like cracks are generally:
options: More critical and judged more strictly by codes
content.explanation: Planar flaws concentrate stress and are typically judged more strictly than rounded volumetric flaws, so correct classification matters for evaluation.
distractors: Planar flaws are not generally acceptable; they are judged strictly.
Planar flaws are detectable when favorably oriented.
Planar cracks differ in severity from rounded porosity.

content.stem: Taking radiographs from more than one angle helps:
options: Detect and characterize flaws that are unfavorably oriented in a single view
content.explanation: Multiple angles improve the chance of aligning a planar flaw with the beam and help characterize size and orientation, addressing RT's orientation sensitivity.
distractors: An IQI is still required on each radiograph.
Each radiograph still requires processing.
Multiple angles do not aim to increase fog.

content.stem: A subtle discontinuity may be missed if the radiograph has:
content.explanation: Low contrast or heavy fog can hide small density differences, so quality requirements exist to make subtle flaws detectable.
distractors: High contrast aids, not hinders, detection.
Proper density supports detection.
Meeting IQI sensitivity supports detection.

content.stem: The main visual cue separating slag from porosity on film is that slag is usually:
options: Irregular and often elongated, while porosity is rounded
content.explanation: Slag images as irregular, frequently elongated dark shapes, whereas porosity is rounded; both are darker than sound metal.
distractors: Slag is typically irregular, not rounded like porosity.
Slag is darker (less dense), not lighter, than the metal.
Slag produces visible indications.

content.stem: Which root-region condition images LIGHTER than the surrounding metal?
content.explanation: Excess root penetration adds metal and images lighter; lack of penetration, concavity, and burn-through all reduce material and image darker.
distractors: Lack of penetration is a gap and images darker.
Root concavity is thinning and images darker.
Burn-through loses metal and images darker.

content.stem: Final accept/reject decisions on radiographs must be made by:
options: Qualified, certified personnel per the applicable procedure and code
content.explanation: Interpretation and evaluation are performed by personnel qualified and certified to the required level, following the governing procedure and acceptance code.
distractors: An untrained observer is not authorized to disposition radiographs.
The welder does not make the certified accept/reject call.
The film manufacturer is not the interpreter.

content.stem: Which statement is correct about radiographic interpretation?
options: Voids image darker, dense inclusions image lighter, and a valid radiograph must precede evaluation
content.explanation: Material loss images darker and dense inclusions lighter, and indications are only evaluated after confirming the radiograph meets quality requirements.
distractors: Voids image darker, not lighter.
Dense inclusions image lighter, not darker.
Radiograph validity is essential before evaluation.

content.stem: On a radiograph, the key difference between a tungsten inclusion and a slag inclusion is that tungsten images:
options: Lighter (denser than the weld), while slag images darker
content.explanation: Tungsten is denser than the weld metal and images lighter, whereas slag is less dense and images darker; the opposite density cues distinguish them.
distractors: Tungsten images lighter, not darker, than slag.
Their densities differ, so they image differently.
Tungsten is a rounded dense inclusion, not a crack.

content.stem: Discontinuity length on a radiograph is commonly measured using:
options: A scale or comparator referenced to the image and known markers
content.explanation: Length is measured directly on the image with a scale or comparator, accounting for any projection, and tied to location markers per the procedure.
distractors: A densitometer measures density, not length.
The kV setting does not measure flaw length.
Source activity is unrelated to sizing.

content.stem: Codes often distinguish scattered porosity from clustered porosity because:
options: Concentration in a small area can be more detrimental to the weld
content.explanation: A dense cluster of pores in a small region can weaken the weld more than the same pores spread out, so acceptance limits address concentration.
distractors: Porosity is judged by size and distribution, not film color.
It does not change the radiation energy.
Clustered porosity is relevant and evaluated.

content.stem: Incomplete penetration and lack of fusion differ in that incomplete penetration is at the:
options: Weld root, while lack of fusion is at the fusion faces between weld and base or passes
content.explanation: Incomplete penetration is a root condition where the joint is not filled, while lack of fusion is unbonding at the fusion faces or between passes; both image as dark linear indications.
distractors: Incomplete penetration is a root condition, not a cap-only one.
Both are subsurface fusion conditions, not surface-only.
They occur at different locations in the joint.

content.stem: Radiography is well suited to volumetric flaws but, compared with ultrasonic testing, is generally less reliable for:
options: Detecting tight, planar flaws oriented across the beam
content.explanation: Tight planar flaws normal to the beam give little radiographic contrast and are better found by UT, while RT excels at volumetric flaws like porosity and slag.
distractors: RT detects porosity well.
RT detects slag well.
RT is fundamentally based on detecting density changes.

content.stem: The roentgen (R) is a unit of:
content.explanation: The roentgen measures ionization produced in air (exposure); absorbed dose uses the rad/gray and dose equivalent uses the rem/sievert.
distractors: Absorbed dose is measured in rad or gray, not roentgens.
Dose equivalent is measured in rem or sievert.
Activity is measured in curies or becquerels.

content.stem: Absorbed dose is measured in:
content.explanation: Absorbed dose (energy deposited per unit mass) is expressed in rad or the SI gray; 1 gray equals 100 rad.
distractors: The roentgen measures exposure in air, not absorbed dose.
The curie measures activity, not dose.
The becquerel measures activity, not dose.

content.stem: Dose equivalent, which accounts for biological effect, is measured in:
content.explanation: Dose equivalent uses the rem or SI sievert; for X and gamma radiation it is numerically close to absorbed dose. 1 sievert equals 100 rem.
distractors: Rad and gray measure absorbed dose, not dose equivalent.
The roentgen measures exposure.
The curie measures activity.

content.stem: One gray is equal to:
content.explanation: 1 gray equals 100 rad by definition; the gray is the SI unit of absorbed dose. (Verify unit relations against current standards.)
distractors: 1 gray is 100 rad, not 1 rad.
1 gray is 100 rad, not 10 rad.
1 gray is 100 rad, not 1000 rad.

content.stem: One sievert is equal to:
content.explanation: 1 sievert equals 100 rem; the sievert is the SI unit of dose equivalent. (Verify unit relations against current standards.)
distractors: 1 sievert is 100 rem, not 1 rem.
1 sievert is 100 rem, not 10 rem.
1 sievert is 100 rem, not 1000 rem.

content.stem: The three cardinal rules of radiation protection are:
content.explanation: Exposure is minimized by reducing time near the source, increasing distance, and using shielding; these are the three cardinal rules.
distractors: Develop, fix, wash are film processing steps, not protection rules.
kV, mA, time are exposure factors, not protection rules.
Source, film, IQI are radiographic components, not protection rules.

content.stem: Reducing the time spent near a radiation source:
content.explanation: Dose accumulates with time at a given dose rate, so less time near the source means proportionally less dose.
distractors: Less time reduces, not increases, dose.
Time directly affects accumulated dose.
Time does not change the source's energy.

content.stem: Increasing distance from a source reduces dose rate according to the:
content.explanation: Dose rate falls with the square of distance, so distance is one of the most effective protective measures.
distractors: Half-life concerns source decay over time, not distance.
Reciprocity relates intensity and time for film exposure.
The characteristic curve relates film density to log exposure.

content.stem: ALARA stands for:
content.explanation: ALARA is the principle of keeping radiation doses as low as reasonably achievable, below regulatory limits, considering technology and cost.
distractors: This is not the meaning of ALARA.
This is not the meaning of ALARA.
This is not the meaning of ALARA.

content.stem: Under US NRC regulations (10 CFR 20), the annual occupational whole-body dose limit is:
content.explanation: 10 CFR 20 sets the occupational whole-body limit at 5 rem (0.05 Sv) per year. (Verify against the current regulation and jurisdiction.)
distractors: 50 rem is ten times the whole-body annual limit.
0.5 rem is closer to the public or declared-pregnant-worker limits, not the general occupational whole-body limit.
500 rem is far above any annual occupational limit.

content.stem: The US NRC annual dose limit for a member of the public is generally:
content.explanation: 10 CFR 20 limits public dose to about 0.1 rem (100 mrem) per year, far below the occupational limit. (Verify against the current regulation.)
distractors: 5 rem is the occupational whole-body limit, not the public limit.
50 rem far exceeds any annual limit.
1 rem is higher than the standard public annual limit.

content.stem: For a declared pregnant worker, the US NRC dose limit to the embryo/fetus over the gestation period is generally:
content.explanation: The limit for the embryo/fetus of a declared pregnant worker is about 0.5 rem (500 mrem) over the gestation period. (Verify against the current regulation.)
distractors: 5 rem is the general occupational whole-body annual limit.
0.1 rem is closer to the annual public limit.
50 rem far exceeds any limit.

content.stem: A 'radiation area' is generally defined as an area where a person could receive a dose rate exceeding:
options: 5 mrem in one hour at 30 cm
5 rem in one hour at 30 cm
content.explanation: Per 10 CFR 20, a radiation area is one where the dose could exceed about 5 mrem in one hour at 30 cm from the source or surface. (Verify against the current regulation.)
distractors: 100 rem in one hour is vastly higher than the radiation-area threshold.
5 rem in one hour at 30 cm is far above the radiation-area threshold.
0.1 mrem in one hour is below the radiation-area threshold.

content.stem: A 'high radiation area' is generally defined as an area where a person could receive a dose rate exceeding:
options: 100 mrem in one hour at 30 cm
content.explanation: Per 10 CFR 20, a high radiation area is one where the dose could exceed about 100 mrem (0.1 rem) in one hour at 30 cm. (Verify against the current regulation.)
distractors: 5 mrem in one hour is the ordinary radiation-area threshold, not high radiation.
1 mrem in one hour is below the radiation-area threshold.
5 rem in one hour is well above the high-radiation-area threshold.

content.stem: A survey meter (such as a Geiger-Mueller or ion chamber instrument) is used to:
options: Measure radiation dose rate in an area
content.explanation: Survey meters read the dose rate at a location, used to establish boundaries and confirm the source is shielded; personal cumulative dose is tracked by dosimeters.
distractors: Cumulative personal dose is recorded by dosimeters, not survey meters.
Survey meters do not develop film.
Survey meters do not set exposure parameters.

content.stem: Compared with a Geiger-Mueller counter, an ion chamber survey meter is generally better for:
content.explanation: Ion chambers handle higher dose-rate fields well, while GM instruments are very sensitive at low levels; the right instrument is chosen for the field.
distractors: Detecting individual low-level counts is a GM strength, not the ion chamber's advantage.
Personal dose recording is done by dosimeters.
Neither instrument develops film.

content.stem: A film badge or TLD/OSL dosimeter is worn to:
options: Record the wearer's accumulated dose over a period
content.explanation: These personnel dosimeters integrate dose over a wear period (often a month) for dose-of-record; they do not give a real-time rate.
distractors: Instantaneous rate is read by survey meters or electronic dosimeters, not the integrating badge of record.
A dosimeter records dose; it does not shield.
A dosimeter does not operate the source.

content.stem: A self-reading pocket dosimeter allows the radiographer to:
options: Check accumulated dose directly during the day
content.explanation: A pocket dosimeter (or electronic dosimeter) gives an immediate read of accumulated dose, useful for managing daily exposure alongside the badge of record.
distractors: Source activity is not measured by a pocket dosimeter.
It does not develop film.
It does not set exposure parameters.

content.stem: An alarming rate meter (audible dosimeter) on a radiographer is required mainly to:
options: Warn immediately if the person enters an unexpectedly high field
content.explanation: An alarming rate meter gives an immediate audible warning of high dose rate (for example an unshielded or stuck source), supplementing but not replacing surveys and dosimeters.
distractors: Dose of record is provided by the badge/TLD, not the alarming rate meter.
It does not measure film density.
It supplements, not replaces, the survey meter.

content.stem: After each gamma radiography exposure, the radiographer must:
options: Survey to confirm the source has fully returned to its shielded position
content.explanation: A survey after each exposure confirms the source is fully retracted and shielded before approaching; this is a core control against overexposure from a stuck source.
distractors: Surveying must never be skipped; it is a primary safety step.
Confirming source position comes before approaching to handle film.
Source activity is fixed by the isotope and is not increased.

content.stem: If a gamma source fails to fully retract (a stuck source), the radiographer should:
options: Maintain distance, keep others away, and follow the emergency procedure
Approach immediately to pull it by hand
content.explanation: A stuck source is a radiation emergency; the radiographer maximizes distance, secures the area, alerts others and the RSO, and follows the written emergency procedure rather than approaching.
distractors: Approaching to grab the source by hand risks a severe overexposure.
A stuck source cannot be ignored; it is an emergency.
Increasing exposure time does not address the hazard and worsens it.

content.stem: Areas where radiography creates elevated dose rates must be:
options: Posted and controlled with appropriate signs and barriers
content.explanation: Restricted and high-radiation areas are posted with caution signs and physically controlled with barriers and surveillance during exposures to keep people out.
distractors: Leaving such areas unmarked endangers personnel.
Elevated-dose areas must be kept clear of the public.
Posting and control must be in place during, not only after, the work.

content.stem: The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) is responsible for:
options: Overseeing the radiation safety program and regulatory compliance
content.explanation: The RSO administers the safety program, training, surveys, dosimetry, and compliance with the license and regulations.
distractors: Film development is a technician task, not the RSO's defining role.
Welding is unrelated to the RSO function.
The RSO oversees safety, not source sales.

content.stem: Industrial radiography in the US is regulated by:
options: The NRC or an Agreement State under equivalent regulations
content.explanation: The NRC regulates byproduct material, with Agreement States enforcing equivalent rules; industrial radiography specifically falls under 10 CFR Part 34 (and state equivalents). (Verify current structure and citations.)
distractors: Radiography is regulated; it is not unregulated.
The film manufacturer does not regulate radiation safety.
ASTM publishes consensus standards but is not the radiation safety regulator.

content.stem: US regulations specific to industrial radiography operations are found primarily in:
content.explanation: 10 CFR Part 34 covers requirements for industrial radiographic operations and equipment, alongside the general radiation protection standards in 10 CFR Part 20. (Verify current citations and any state equivalents.)
distractors: Part 20 gives general protection standards; Part 34 is the radiography-specific part.
ASTM E94 is a consensus practice, not the federal radiography regulation.
A film data sheet is not a regulation.

content.stem: Requiring both a calibrated survey meter and an alarming rate device reflects the principle of:
options: Independent means to detect a source out of shield
content.explanation: Using more than one independent indicator reduces the chance that an unshielded or stuck source goes undetected, a defense-in-depth safety practice.
distractors: These devices are safety instruments, not film processing aids.
They do not change the radiation energy.
The purpose is safety redundancy, not merely cost.

content.stem: Ionizing radiation can harm tissue because it:
options: Ionizes atoms and can damage cells and DNA
content.explanation: Ionizing radiation deposits energy that can break molecular bonds and damage DNA, which is the basis of dose limits and ALARA.
distractors: The hazard is ionization and cellular damage, not mere harmless warming.
Radiation does interact with tissue.
Ionizing radiation can harm, not improve, cell function.

content.stem: For a high-energy gamma source like Co-60, effective shielding generally requires:
options: Greater thickness of dense material than for a lower-energy source
content.explanation: Higher-energy gammas have larger half-value layers, so more dense shielding (such as thick lead or steel/concrete) is needed than for lower-energy sources.
distractors: High-energy sources require substantial shielding, not none.
A thin lead foil is inadequate for Co-60 energies.
Plastic sheeting provides negligible shielding for high-energy gammas.

content.stem: The official dose of record for a radiographer is normally provided by:
options: A processed personnel dosimeter (film badge, TLD, or OSL)
content.explanation: The dose of record comes from the evaluated personnel dosimeter (badge/TLD/OSL) read by a processor; pocket and electronic dosimeters support daily management but the badge is the record.
distractors: Pocket dosimeters support daily checks but are not usually the legal dose of record.
A survey meter measures area dose rate, not personal cumulative dose.
An exposure chart is a technique aid, not a dose record.

content.stem: Documents such as ASTM E94 and E1742 provide:
options: Standard practices for performing and documenting radiographic examination
content.explanation: ASTM E94 (guide for radiographic examination) and E1742 (practice for radiographic examination) give consensus practice requirements; dose limits come from the regulations (10 CFR). (Verify current revisions.)
distractors: Federal dose limits are set by regulation (10 CFR), not these ASTM practices.
Source licensing is a regulatory matter, not the content of these practices.
Developer formulas are not the subject of these standards.
